In this way, Fornell et al. [78] investigated the effects of annealing treatments on the microstructure, elastic/mechanical properties, wear resistance and corrosion behavior of rod-shaped Ti40Zr10Cu38Pd12, they found that the amorphous alloy exhibits large hardness, relatively low Young’s modulus, good wear resistance and excellent corrosion behavior. Nanoindentation measurements reveal that the sample annealed in the supercooled liquid region exhibits a hardness value of 9.4 GPa, which is 20% larger than in the completely amorphous state and much larger than the hardness of commercial Ti–6Al–4V alloy. The Young’s modulus of the as-cast alloy (around 100 GPa) increases only slightly during partial crystallization. Finally, the anticorrosion performance of the Ti40Zr10Cu38Pd12 alloy in Hank’s solution has been shown to ameliorate as crystallization proceeds and is roughly as good as in the commercial Ti–6Al–4V alloy.

Over the last years, copper bus-bars have gained an important market share in electrical and electronic applications, especially in the Asia-Pacific region.

### **MICROSTRUCTURE AND MECHANICAL PROPERTIES OF ULTRA FINE GRAINED HIGH PERFORMANCE COPPER ALLOYS** 

H.-A. Kuhn, I. Altenberger, J. Riedle, H. Hцlzl _Wieland-Werke AG Central Laboratory, Research & Development Graf-Arco-Str. 36 89079 Ulm, Germany achim.kuhn@wieland.de_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Ultra fine grained (UFG) _pure_ copper has been thoroughly investigated in the last two decades, however ultra fine grained high-strength copper _alloys_ have scarcely been characterized so far. This contribution puts focus on UFG copper alloys, more specifically, Cu-Ni-Si alloys, being well known as ideal materials for electromechanical connectors, springs and lead frames. Characterization of these materials after severe plastic deformation and subsequent aging was carried out using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), conductivity, hardness and tensile test measurements. The results show that UFG low alloyed copper alloys exhibit impressive combinations of properties such as strength plus conductivity plus high ductility and acceptable thermal stability at low and medium temperatures. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

130 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Precipitation hardened Cu-Ni-Si alloys are a well established and technologically important class of materials for a wide range of applications where high strength and good conductivity are required. In contrast to other strengthening methods such as solid solution hardening, severe plastic deformation leads only to a weak decrease of conductivity and is therefore a means of enhancing strength while maintaining acceptable conductivity for current bearing parts and components. By a subsequent aging treatment the severely plastically deformed microstructure can be further enhanced and thermal stability can profit from grain-boundary pinning by precipitated nanoscale nickel silicides. 

### **SEVERE PLASTIC DEFORMATION BY SWAGING** 

Similar to Equal Channel Angular Pressing (ECAP), swaging (or rotary swaging) and subsequent precipitation hardening is a simple method for producing ultra fine grained precipitation hardened copper alloys. Swaging is suitable for producing continuous semi-finished materials such as wires. Figs. 1 and 2 exhibit the grain structure of ultra fine grained CuNi3Si1Mg as obtained by electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD) in the scanning electron microscope (SEM).

Optimized severe plastic deformation of wires by swaging with sufficiently high cold work leads to ultra fine grained microstructures exhibiting grain sizes of 0.2 to 0.5 microns after peak aging at 450°C/1h. It can be confirmed by misorientation measurements using EBSD that the observed grain boundaries in swaged CuNi3Si1Mg (UNS-designation 70250) wire (diameter 2,7 mm) are in fact high-angle grain boundaries (misorientation between adjacent grains > 10°). In addition, within the ultra fine grains some low-angle grain boundaries (red colour, Fig. 2) can be detected by EBSD. 

Through a combination of swaging and optimized precipitation hardening, an ultra fine grained precipitation hardened grain structure (Fig. 3) can be generated with nanoscale Ni-silicide precipitates situated predominantly at or near grain boundaries, thus pinning the grain boundaries and enhancing the thermal stability at elevated temperatures. An alternative severe plastic deformation method for strip materials is accumulative roll bonding (ARB). Accumulative roll bonding as a severe plastic deformation technique was successfully applied in laboratory scale on pure copper strips [1,2] and on dispersion and dispersion hardened Cu-Fe1-P [3]. ### **CONCLUSION /SUMMARY** 

Rotary Swaging or accumulative roll bonding are two very efficient processes to generate high strength through ultra fine grains, especially if they are combined with precipitation hardening.  EBSD and electron channeling contrast in the SEM are very helpful tools to characterize such tempers. 

Both, swaging and accumulative roll bonding, typically lead to  a maximum hardness at a logarithmic strain or deformation degree of 2.5 and 5, respectively. 

Severely plastically deformed (swaged or accumulative roll bonded) and subsequently precipitation hardened Cu-Ni-Si-Mg alloys show only slightly earlier softening than conventionally rolled microstructures. Grain boundary pinning by nanoscopically small precipitates is suggested as the underlying mechanism.

### **CORROSION, ANTIFOULING PROPERTIES, FATIGUE AND WEAR OF COPPER ALLOYS FOR SEAWATER APPLICATIONS** 

J. Aufrecht, A. Grohbauer and U.Hofmann _Wieland-Werke AG Graf-Arco-Str. 36 D-89079 Ulm, Germany jochen.aufrecht@wieland.de_ 

A. Drach, I. Tsukrov, J. DeCew _Mechanical Engineering Department University of New Hampshire Durham, NH 03824, USA_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Copper alloys are widely used in marine applications because of their very good resistance to corrosion and biofouling. A promising new application is the use of copper alloys as wire material for fishnets in marine aquaculture cages. In this paper, a series of laboratory and field studies to evaluate the suitability of different copper alloys for this application is discussed. 

The corrosion resistance in artificial and natural seawater is investigated by weight loss measurements and optical microscopy. Most alloys show a very good corrosion resistance. The measured uniform corrosion rates decrease with the duration of testing and reach values lower than 50 µm/year after 3-4 months of exposure. Neither selective corrosion nor dealloying are detected from the natural seawater tests. However, the data from artificial seawater tests indicates that the alloys with low susceptibility to dealloying perform better. 

The biofouling resistance of most tested alloys is very good: the observed weight gains due to biomass accumulation are under 0.5%. However, the aluminum-alloyed brass specimens exhibit relatively high levels of biofouling (weight gain of 45%), thus

indicating that some alloying elements can significantly reduce the biofouling resistance of copper alloys. 

Fatigue and wear performance of copper alloys in wire form is investigated in artificial seawater using the custom-designed testing equipment. The obtained data indicates that the mechanical performance of copper alloys strongly depends on the type of the alloy (brass vs. copper-nickel), diameter and temper (hard vs. soft). 

The collected data on seawater performance of copper alloys confirms that these materials are suitable for use in seawater applications. In particular, it appears that admiralty brasses are the most suitable type of copper alloys for marine aquaculture, based on their performance characteristics and relatively low cost of the alloying elements.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper alloys are excellent materials for seawater applications due to their good corrosion resistance on the one hand and biofouling resistance on the other [1-8]. Typical examples of alloys used in marine environments are tin bronzes, copper-nickel and copper-aluminum alloys, and brasses (including tin-alloyed admiralty and naval brasses). 

Even though copper alloys have been mainly used for piping and cladding applications in seawater environment, recently these materials have been introduced into marine aquaculture. This quickly growing industry uses polymer netting for fish containment in fish cages, analogous to the nets traditionally used for fishing. However, polymers (e.g. polyester and nylon) have some major drawbacks in this application, including strength that is insufficient to prevent loss of fish due to predation (e.g. seals or sharks biting through the net), and biofouling that leads to relatively fast accumulation of biomass and blockage of water flow through the netting. Both issues can lead to significant economical damage to fish farming operations due to the loss of fish, slowdown of fish growth rates and increased sensitivity if fish to diseases and vermin. As a consequence, frequent and expensive cleaning and integrity evaluation procedures are necessary for the fish cages with polymer netting. 

Copper alloys present a promising alternative for use as netting material in marine aquaculture, because they exhibit higher strength and resistant to biofouling, when compared to polymers. Studies evaluating the use of copper alloy netting in marine aquaculture report positive results [9,10]. However, copper alloy nets used for this application are subjected to a complex combination of service loads, such as: cyclic and impact stresses, seawater corrosion, wear. 

To evaluate the suitability of different copper alloys for use in marine aquaculture, a combination of laboratory and field studies were conducted to determine the corrosion and biofouling resistance, and fatigue and wear behavior in seawatersubmerged conditions. In this paper, the authors discuss the experimental procedur

es and summarize the results from this testing program.

The two exceptions are the nickel silver alloy C764 with a corrosion rate of 28 µm/year, and the aluminum brass C688 with rate of 4 µm/year. At the same time, the aluminum brass is the only tested alloy that exhibits high level of biofouling (similar to that of tested steel specimens), while other alloys show high biofouling resistance. Metallographic survey of the corroded sample shows that the localized corrosion is limited to relatively shallow pits without detectable dealloying or selective corrosion damage. Comparison of the data from laboratory and field tests indicates that high-copper alloys show a similar corrosion behavior in both artificial and natural seawater, while brasses and copper-nickels show significant differences in the corrosion kinetics between the two environments. This suggests that natural seawater testing is necessary for accurate evaluation of the seawater performance of the latter two types of copper alloys. The largest difference between natural and artificial seawater exposures is observed in the corrosion rates of nickel silver alloy C764. This phenomenon requires a more detailed investigation. Fatigue and wear performance of copper alloys in seawater environment is _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 150 investigated using the custom-bu

ilt testing equipment. The obtained data indicates that the mechanical performance of copper alloys strongly depends on the type of the alloy and temper. The collected data on corrosion, fatigue and wear allows to perform service life predictions for components made of copper alloys in seawater applications, such as marine aquaculture. The testing approach discussed in this paper has a potential to accelerate development of technical specifications and reduce the time-to-market for new alloys and wire products. 

Comparison of the relative performance of the tested alloys lead to a conclusion that the admiralty brasses have the best combination of the performance characteristics for the use as a wire material in marine aquaculture. Furthermore, relatively low cost of the alloying elements makes this alloy the most suitable for this application from engineering and economical perspectives.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

In the modern day the development of new and high performance materials is significant and interesting to produce. Copper is widely used in engineering applications because of its properties, such as, resistance to corrosion, electrical and/or thermal conductivity, good fatigue resistance and easy fabrication [1,2]. However, copper has the disadvantage of low mechanical strength. But its strength can be increased by adding alloying elements of (e.g. Mo) by forming a solid solution. Interesting alloys are Cu-Mo alloys, which are used in applications of heat sink material, vacuum technology and electronic packing devices due to their physical and electronic properties [2,3]. In most of the applications, high-density Cu-Mo materials with homogeneous microstructures are required for high performance. [3]. The disadvantage of Cu-Mo systems is that they present a positive mixing enthalpy at solid state [4], thus the solubility of Mo in Cu at room temperature is negligible [4]. But it is known that by using a non-equilibrium process, such as mechanical

alloying (MA), the range of solubility of many systems can be extended [5,6]. MA is a simple and versatile process that transfers high amounts of energy from milling balls to the alloy powders during the milling process [6]. MA is a dry, solid-state powder processing technique (a liquid medium can also be used sometimes during milling operations) which involves repeated welding, fracturing and re-welding of powder particles in a high-energy ball mill [6]. It allows the range of solubility to be extended and also allows the solubility in immiscible binary systems to be obtained [6,7]. During MA, intense deformation is introduced into the particles, which is manifested by the increase of crystalline defects, such as dislocation, stacking faults, and increased number of crystallite boundaries. The presence of crystalline defects increases the Gibbs free energy and the Gibbs free energy curves are moved upwards; hence the solubility limit changes. [8,9]. Furthermore, by MA it is possible to obtain nanocrystalline materials (NCM), which are very interesting, because they exhibit an unusual combination of properties such as strength, good ductility, high fracture toughness, and good corrosion resistance. [6]. These new and unsuspected chemical and physical properties are not found in coarse-grained materials [10]. This paper is a resume of the research work of our group [11-14] about Cu-Mo alloys and gives results of analyze and characterize the synthesis of nanocrystalline Cu-xMo alloys (x= 1, 3, 5 and 8 wt.%) by means of MA and to discuss the solid solution extension of Mo into Cu.

The experiments were performed using Cu powders at 99.% Cu, containing less than 1000 ppm of oxygen. The particle sizes ranged between 170 and 400 mesh for Cu and 325 and 400 mesh for Mo. The milling operation was carried out on powder blends of Cu-xMo (x= 1, 3, 5 and 8 wt.%) and the mixture was placed in a 25 ml hardened steel vial and milled in a SPEX 8000D mill with argon for 0.5, 4, 8 and 50 h. Hardened steel balls of 12.5  mm diameters with a constant ball/powder ratio of 10/1 were used as the milling media, and 1wt.% of stearic acid was used as the process control agent. The x-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was conducted in a Siemens D5000 diffractometer with copper radiation and annealing pure copper was used as the standard. All the patterns

When solute atoms are dissolved into the solid solution, they increase the hardness, which increases the fragmentation tendency [21]. Smaller crystallite sizes are around of 10 nm at 50 h of milling for the Cu-Mo alloys; hence, all alloys have a nanocrystalline structure. Nanostructures are formed by the deformation that occurs in shear bands located in unstrained grains. The crystalline size decreases steadily and the shear band coalesces when milling time increases. The small angle boundaries are replaced by higher angle grain boundaries, implying grain rotation which produces disclinations [22]. This is reflected by the absence of texture in the electron diffraction pattern and random orientation of the observed grains,(contributing to x-ray peak diffraction broadening) from the lattice fringes in the high resolution electron images. Thus, dislocation free nanocrystalline grains are formed. As milling continues, the nanocrystalline grains reach a saturation value. Due to the difficulty of dislocation generation at the nanocrystalline size, the existing dislocations will rearrange and some become eliminated. For this reason, the strain and dislocation density decreases. In nanocrystalline materials, the grain size can coincide with crystallite size, due to the fact that the crystallite size is the smallest scale length in a microstructure. In Figure 3a shows Gibbs free energy as a function of milling time, and it can be observed that free energy increases due to the creation of new interfaces caused by the reduction of crystallite size. At 50 h of milling the Gibbs free energy values produced by increasing of crystallite boundary increases around 3-4 kJ/mol for all Cu-Mo alloys. Finally, Figure 3b shows that dislocation density increases with milling time, until typical values of materials with severe plastic deformation decrease [23,24], and then the dislocation density decreases slightly, as mentioned above. At 50 h of milling the Gibbs free energy values produced by increasing the elastic strain energy due to the presence of dislocations increases around 1-2 kJ/mol for all Cu-Mo alloys. For the industry in general and for the mining and metallurgical industry in particular, wastes and residues generated during their activities have strongly changed the perception of the human being. 

It will not comprehensible today to find an institution in the world, ca

pable to use a chimney leaving gases to the atmosphere, as image of development and economical growing, as it was years ago. For our modern society, a change of paradigms is in the mind of most part of the people who is putting the more and more attention in the environment effects of our industrial activities. Today is not only necessary to produce new products for the human welfare, but also to take account in how are they being produced and how much this production impact into the neighbouring. In this way, recycling and reuse of wastes is welcome today, as these wastes could be considered as new resources.

Just to think, in the case of copper extraction, only around 1% of the resource will be used and around 99% must be disposed. However today slag and tailing are considering as new resources for uses in alternative purposes as material construction, par example. In this form, we will be able to diminish largely those big quantities of residues generated during copper primary production. 

Additionally, a fort increase of secondary material utilization has coming very frequent. Secondary material, containing copper and its alloys after primary use is definitely part of the new copper resources which begin to play an important role in the whole metal production in the world. The so called “urban mining” is already taking place in all main consumer countries as those European and North Americans. 

Papers grouped in this chapter is an equilibrated balance between primary and secondary wastes generated in the world, which certainly corresponds to the participation in this event of the main copper producer and consumer of the society.

### **ABSTRACT** 

Chilean copper is produced by two processes: concentrators on the basis of physical separation technology, including mining, crushing, milling and flotation, obtaining concentrates (typically 28-35% Cu), and hydrometallurgical plants, including mining, crushing, heap leaching, solvent extraction and electrowinning, obtaining copper cathodes (99.99% Cu). A portion of the concentrates is treated in smelters and ele

ctrorefineries, obtaining copper cathodes (99.99% Cu), while another portion is exported to be treated in international facilities. 

Typical wastes generated during these local processes are acid drainage, flotation tailings, copper slag, smelter flue dusts, acid effluents, etc. 

In the last few decades, the local copper industry has implemented several technologies and carried out research to manage these wastes and recover metals that contain mainly copper, molybdenum, and iron, among others. 

This paper reviews the present situation regarding waste management in the Chilean copper industry in terms of generation and characterization, as well as the operations and research carried out to recover metals from these wastes. Some suggestions are made regarding waste management and metal recovery guidelines and regulations to increase the chain value in the mining and metallurgical copper recovery process.

However, the private mine Escondida is the biggest single copper producer (1.1 Mt/y), while other important operations are Los Pelambres (418 kt/y), Minera Sur Andes (417 kt/y), Collahuasi (282 kt/y), Esperanza (173 kt/y), Spence (167 kt/y), El Abra (154 kt/y), and Candelaria (123 kt/y), among others  1  . 

Furthermore, Chile is a globally important producer and exporter of molybdenum, a by-product obtained from copper processing, as well as of gold, silver, industrial minerals like sodium and potassium nitrate, iodine, lithium, and borates  1  . 

In terms of copper reserves, Chile accounts for 24% of the world total, which reached 680 Mton in 2012. Additionally, the country ranked number one in terms of worldwide exploration expenditure for copper, with 15% (690 Million US$) for the same year  2  . 

The Chilean Copper Commission (COCHILCO) forecast over US$ 103 billion in mining investments for the 2013 – 2010 p

eriod, where over 70% is related to copper initiatives. This should increase copper production to over 8 Mton by 2020  2  . Generally, Chilean copper is produced by two ways: - Concentrators, based on physical upgrading technology, including mining extraction, crushing, milling, and flotation, obtaining concentrates (typically 2835% Cu). A portion of these concentrates is treated in smelters and electro- _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 173 refineries, obtaining copper cathodes (99.99% Cu), while another portion is exported to be treated in international facilities. - Hydrometallurgical plants, including mining extraction, crushing, heap leaching, solvent extraction and electro winning, obtaining copper cathodes (99.99% Cu). Several wastes are generated during these processes, which must be managed and disposed of in order to meet the standards and regulations passed by the Chilean government. Additionally, local industry has implemented several technologies and carried out research to treat these wastes and to recover the metals they contain, as well as to dispose of dangerous impurities safely and thus to achieve waste minimization. In this context, this paper reviews the present situation regarding waste management in the Chilean copper industry in terms of generation and characterization, as well as summarizing operations and research carried out to recover metals from these wastes. ### **ENVIRONMENTAL REGULATIONS** Since 1991, several environmental regulations have been established by the Chilean government in order to reduce emissions to the atmosphere, water (river, sea and lakes) and to the soil, as well as to manage wastes generated. ### <u>Liquid Effluents from acid plant</u> 

Sulfuric acid plants generate arsenic-containing effluents, which are treated in effluent treatment plants. Normally, the solution is neutralized and arsenic is precipitated as calcium arsenite, CaAsO2OH, and calcium arsenate, Ca2AsO4(OH). In addition, calcination is used to produce a stable product, Ca3(AsO4)2  16  . However, this process normally generates a treated effluent with a high content of As (about 150 ppm), as well as a large quantity of arsenical residues to be disposed of. 

In this context, EcoMetales Limited is working on a new process to be used at the acid plant in Codelco’s El Teniente Division, where today arsenic bearing acid effluent is being treated with lime, obtaining a treated effluent with a residual As concentration and a significant quantity of solid arsenical waste. The new proposal includes As precipitation as As2S3 using sulphidric acid generated _in situ_ in bioreactors. This plant should process around 700 m<sup>3</sup> /d of effluent to obtain a treated effluent with a very low level of residual As, while the quantity of solid arsenical residue should be reduced in quantity by 4 times, as compared to lime treatment.

### **THE ECONOMIC POTENTIAL OF TAILINGS** 

R.L. Mallea Correa _K-UTEC AG, Salt Technologies, Germany 99706 Sondershausen Am Petersenschacht 7 rmallea@gmail.com_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Copper production in Chile is associated with the generation of great quantities of massive residuals, such as gravel, slag and tailings. For example, the copper

industry has generated approximately 2,156 million tons of tailings during the last ten years (20022011). The future trend is the growing generation of residuals per ton produced of copper concentrate. The tailings generated by flotation plants present interesting concentrations of elements such as iron, aluminum, lead, selenium, tellurium, tungsten, rhenium, and rare earths, among others. 

The increasing demand of many of these elements, at the international level, along with the high prices of the same, confer a commercial value to such residuals, turning them into secondary raw materials with an important business potential. These elements contain key components and strategic raw materials for the maintenance and development of new and advanced technologies that allow for or facilitate the economic welfare of industrialized countries. Most of these industrialized European Union countries, besides the U.S.A. and Japan, have explicitly recognized that the lack of certain elements – which are being produced mainly by China, Russia, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Brazil – represents a great challenge for the management of their finances. 

The above should catch the attention either of the public and private sectors in Chile, in order to develop initiatives aimed at turning such potentialities in tangible business opportunities to generate a greater welfare for Chile.

### **<mark>OVERVIEW</mark>** 

The mining production in Chile is associated to the generation of great amounts of massive residuals, such as slag, gravels, and tailings, among others. Only between years 2002 to 2011, there was generated approximately 2,156 million tons of tailings, and it currently exist about 870 tailing ponds, most of which are inactive at present. 

The copper producers in Chile are divided into: Large Scale Mining industry, that has produced among 90% to 94% of the national total during the last 7 years; MediumScale Mining industry, producing between 5% to 7%; and the Small-Scale Mining industry, which produces about 1% of such total (SERNAGEOMIN[1]). 

Chile possesses one of the major copper mineralization in the world, and it has been proved, as per Oyarzъn [2], that there exist mainly three types of deposits: the **veinshaped** deposits, the **porphyry-copper** deposits and the **strata-bound** deposits. The firsts are characterized by the presence of copper in the form of high-grade ore veins, corresponding to oxide ore, mainly in the form of Atacamite, cuprite, chrisocole and brochantite. 

The second, and quiet abundant in Los Andes mountain range but of a lower grade, correspond to sulfide ores, with presence of chalcopyrite, covellite, bornite, enargite and chalcocite. ### **SEA DISPOSAL OF MINE TAILINGS FROM COPPER MINING – AN ALTERNATIVE TO LAND DISPOSAL** 

### J.M.Skei 

_Skei Mining Consultant (SMC) Bassengveien 7A, 2006 Lшvenstad, Norway jens@skeimining.com_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Mineral production generates tailings and waste rock in large quantities and due to lack of sufficient beneficial use, the mineral residues are considered as waste material which has to be disposed. Management of large amounts of solid waste is a logistical and environmental challenge and the permits for mining are dependent on what is considered as environmental acceptable waste management. The definition of what is acceptable has been unclear and the consequence is that the mining companies experience a considerable unpredictability in terms of waste handling and permissions. Mines located not far from the sea should consider and explore deep sea disposal (DSTP) of tailings and waste rock as an alternative to land disposal. Many coastal states, Norway included, have either applied or planned sea disposal of tailings. Lack of suitable land disposal sites due to conflicting interests of land use has increased the need of exploring the possibility of DSTP. However, sea disposal is a political sensitive issue and among environmentalists strong opposition has been expressed. Alternative disposal sites should be evaluated and decisions should be based on an overall impact assessment where land areas and the marine environment are compared. Site specific conditions will influence environmental risks and user conflicts. Consequently, environmental acceptance criteria and criteria for classification of suitability for disposal sites are needed. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

196 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Management of large amounts of solid waste is an environmental challenge [1] and the permits for mining are to a large extent dependent on what is considered as environmentally acceptable. So far the definition of what is accep

table has been unclear and the consequence is that the mining companies experience a considerable unpredictability in terms of waste handling and permissions [2]. Acceptable risk is the environmental effects which are considered acceptable for the environment and stakeholders.Therefore a set of acceptance criteria based on scientific evaluations should be developed for mine waste disposal on land and in the sea to be able to compare risks. 

Large scale mining operations will inevitably create environmental footprints. The challenge is to minimize the footprints to achieve acceptable waste management in the mining industry. There are several factors influencing the impact of waste disposal, such as the volume of solid waste to be handled, the geochemical, physical and the toxicological  characteristics of the waste. Additionally, site specific conditions play an important role and the disposal infrastructure and the technology applied to manage the waste. Use of Best Available Technology (BAT) is a good principle, but its applicability will to a large extent be site specific. What works in one location may not necessarily work elsewhere. 

The objective of this paper is to discuss the environmental challenges related to solid waste management in the mining industry, with emphases on copper mines and sea disposal of mineral waste. A case history will be presented, including material from a recent EIA study of alternative waste disposal from a planned copper mine in Northern Norway (Nussir ASA). Only solid waste material will be considered in this paper. 

### **WASTE MANAGEMENT PRINCIPLES** 

Solid waste products in mining consist of waste rock, which need to be removed from the mine site to get access to the ore, and tailings which is the fine grained material (clay to sand) produced during the extraction (i.e. flotation) of metals or minerals. Both waste products are produced in large volumes and carefully planned disposal alternatives should be presented early in the project planning. If not the progress of the project implementation may be slowed down or halted, due to environmental scrutiny. 

Principally, there are at least three alternative ways of handling solid waste in the mining industry: 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

197 

1. Backfilling of solid waste in abandoned open pits or underground mine shafts. 

2. Disposal in natural or artificial lakes; with or without permanent water cover. 

3. Disposal in the sea – shallow (< 100m) or deep (> 100m). 

In addition to those three alternatives it is a continuous effort from the mining industry to invent and explore solutions where the solid waste material no longer may be considered as waste, but as a useful product with an economic potential. The status is that a certain fraction of the solid waste, particularly waste rock may be utilized, but due to the enormous volumes of solid waste it is not realistic to consider a mining industry with no solid waste disposal. In the

future the technology of extracting metals and minerals may change and the amount of waste products may be reduced. Waste minimization is a goal in all human activities. 

Regarding legislation practices in Europe see EU Mineral Waste Directive (2006/21/EC)) 

http://europa.eu/legislation_summaries/environment/waste_management/l28134_en.htm and EU Reference Document on Best Available Techniques for Management of Tailings and Waste-Rock in Mining Activities, http://eippcb.jrc.ec.europa.eu/reference/mmr.html 

The international practice regarding solid waste management varies. In some way the choice of alternatives is site specific, in some way politically determined. Surprisingly, the choice of disposal practice is to a little extent based on solid scientific documentation. This is particularly the case when comparing the environmental impact of land disposal and sea disposal. Emotional attitudes play a substantial role when considering sea disposal. When it comes to land disposal this is a practice which has been operating for a long time and the negative environmental effects have to a large extent been traditionally accepted by the public. It is therefore a need of looking at disposal alternatives in a wider perspective and to compare advantages and disadvantages for the total environment (land, sea, resources and humans) in a short and long time perspective. This comparison must be based on facts and scientific documentation and not on emotion and opportunism. To achieve this, the mining companies and research councils must support scientific programs where the results are published in peer-review journals. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

### **DISPOSAL SITE CHARACTERIZATION** 

In all circumstances it is important to obtain a detailed knowledge about the disposal site and its surroundings, whether the site is on land or in the sea. Consequently, comprehensive base line studies are necessary with focus on natural variability of environmental quality and efforts to understand the processes influencing variability [3].The base line study is the platform for future monitoring where the impact of disposal of mine waste is to be documented and reported. Natural variability (seasonal and inter annual) concerns both on land locations and sea locations. Climatic change has created a new situation regarding land sites, characterized by violent weather (heavy storms, huge water rainfalls, flooding, landslides etc.). Establishing large dam systems for tailing in areas exposed to unpredictable effects of climate changes may be a considerable challenge (see fig.1).Consequently, new dams established in such areas may need careful design to avoid risks related to dam failure with dramatic consequences.

### **NUSSIR ASA – A NEW COPPER INITIATIVE IN NORWAY** 

NUSSIR ASA is a mining company established in 2005 in Northern Norway. The Nussir Field was discovered in the 1970's and remains to be one of Norway's major undeveloped copper deposits. Further exploration of its ore has yielded valuable amounts of gold, silver, platinum and palladium in addition to its significant copper deposits. Nussir plan to use a sea-deposit for their tailings, effectively removing the problem of acid mine drainage. Also the minerals surrounding the copper bearing minerals contains little or no sulphides (such as pyrite), making the tailings much less troublesome for the environment. The ore deposit is located close to a fjord and a lot of technical infrastructure is on place due to mining activities between 1972 and 1979 (fig.2). 













Figure 2 – The mine site of Nussir ASA. The ore body is located in the mountain behind the old mining buildings and the fjord, Repparfjord, is in front (photo: Geir Dahl-Hansen, Akvaplan-niva) 

The ore contains about 1.1 % copper and the predominant minerals are bornite, chalcocite and chalcopyrite. The ore body is estimated to contain about 26 million tonnes of copper. 

The mine site location does not favor land disposal of tailings, partly due to the geomorphology and partly due to potential conflicts with reindeer herding by the Sami people. Consequently, sea disposal of tailings has been evaluated in a major Environmental Impact Study (EIA) submitted in 2011. One of the important issues has been dispersal and sedimentation of tailing particles in the fjord and the environmental

Additionally, the tailing characteristics (physically, chemically as well as toxic potential) and modeling of particle dispersal and sedimentation, were carried out.

One of the explanations of why the sedimentation of the tailings takes place so close to the discharge pipe is the grain size of the tailings (fig.6). 











Figure 6 – The grain size distribution of the tailings from Nussir ASA, prior to flocculation[5] 

Only 25% of the tailing particles are <20µm, which are considered as the fines, which easily get dispersed in water. However, as long as the fine tailing is disposed in seawater an efficient flocculation process takes place and the settling rate increases [6]. In seawater most of the natural mineral particles are in a flocculated state and the size of the aggregates often exceeds 250 µm [7]. Sea water is a perfect environment for clustering individual particles — the water is of high salinity (>30 ppt), and is rich in both particulate and dissolved organic matter.  The main encounter mechanisms are differential settling (large particles sinking quickly will sweep up the smaller particles), and laminar or turbulent shear where differences in fluid velocity cause two particles carried by the fluid to approach each other.  High particle concentration helps both encounter mechanisms[6]. In fjords influenced by glacial flour extraordinary high levels may occur in the melting season [8].This implies that high turbidity water near a tailing outfall will also facilitate flocculation. 

The EIA study concluded that during a production period of 25 years about 20 tonnes of copper and 3.4 tonnes of nickel will be discharged to the fjord. The tailing will contain between 320 and 670 mg/kg copper. Modeling of particle dispersal indicates moderate increase of turbidity in the near surface water. Some release of copper and nickel from the tailing deposit will appear, however, the levels of dissolved metals in the

water column will be low due to dilution caused by frequent exchange of bottom water [5]. 

Deposition of tailings is expected to influence areas of fish spawning. However, the disposal site only account for about 20%

of the bottom area of the fjord and the consequences are moderate. The impact of sea disposal of tailings on salmon was also investigated. Modeling of toxicity with respect to salmon due to elevated concentrations of copper in the water indicate no problem as the concentrations in water are far below both acute and chronic limits of toxicity of copper [5]. 

### **ENVIRONMENTAL ACEPTANCE CRITERIA** 

To avoid that tailings disposal will be a stopper of planned mining projects; a roadmap for waste management should be discussed and agreed upon in a preliminary phase of every mine project.Disposal of mine tailings in the sea is considered by many as not appropriate due to the potential environmental risk. However, little focus has been on the difference between acceptable and non-acceptable risk [2]. Scientific criteria for suitable disposal sites and acceptance criteria for environmental impact are unfortunately missing. 

Acceptance criteria represent a specific and defined list of conditions that must be met before a project will be accepted by the assigning parties.It is important that stakeholders take part in the process of developing acceptance criteria to ensure that the disposal is conducted with minimum negative impacts in both short term and long term [2]. Based on a common agreement that mining will have a negative effect on the environment related to tailings disposal, the next relevant question is whether the negative impact can be accepted or not. This implies that the negative effects must be put in perspective. When the impact from tailing disposal is assessed it is important to consider the magnitude of influence and for how long. More quantitative assessments, either by modeling or field verification must be applied. Comprehensive monitoring programs are necessary to assess the natural variability to be able to evaluate the impact of mine waste disposal in the sea. This suggests that acceptance criteria are needed to distinguish between anticipated effects based on assumptions and real effects based on scientific documentation. 

Two specific acceptance criteria may be mentioned. Tailing disposal in seawater creates increased turbidity within a certain distance from the tailing pipe outlet. What may be accepted as maximum turbidity to avoid negative consequences for fish at different life stages?  Tailing disposal causes hyper sedimentation in a certain distance from the tailing pipe. What is the maximum annual sedimentation rate of tailings which may be considered acceptable to maintain a sediment bottom fauna? It is well known 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

204 

from literature that bottom fauna disappears where massive sedimentation of tailings takes place, but less information exists about the impact on the fauna in the surroundings of a disposal site where a moderate amount of tailings deposits. This is important to assess the area of influence. It should be emphasized that the negative effect on the sea b

ottom fauna is partly temporal, even in the main disposal area [3]. When the mine is closed and the disposal of tailings terminate natural sedimentation gradually rehabilitate the tailings surface and provide organic matter for a new seabed and provide livelihood for a new habitat. 

These are examples where an effort has to be made to establish acceptance criteria, either by investigating existing disposal sites or closed sites. Additionally, useful quantitative information may be obtained by experimental work. 

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Large scale mining creates environmental challenges. Waste management plans should include alternatives, both with respect to land disposal and sea disposal, if relevant. Copper mining involving sulfide minerals and acid mine drainage are particularly relevant in terms of sea disposal due to the buffer capacity of seawater and the efficiency of flocculation of fine tailings particles in seawater. However, the metal content of tailings and waste rock and the mobility of the metals should be documented and become a part of the acceptance criteria. It is of outmost importance to come to an agreement and common understanding of the waste management issues in the early planning of a mining project to achieve a predictable process. Sea disposal is demanding because limited amount of environmental data are published in the open literature. 

Natural variability is one important issue when monitoring the environment and interpretation of data take place. Use of statistics is crucial. Understanding of natural processes in the sea is another. The mechanism of flocculation of fine grained mineral particles in the sea has in many cases been overlooked. This is very essential when prediction of particle dispersal and sedimentation of mine tailings is to be assessed, as well as estimating the size of the area of influence.

### **FLUID BED ROASTING OF FAYALITE SLAG – THEORETICAL ANALYSIS** 

Mario Sanchez _Universidad Andres Bello, Chile mario.sanchez@unab.cl_ 

Michael Sudbury _Metallurgical Consultant, Oakville, Ontario, Canada msudbury@cogeco.ca_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Small scale tests have shown it is possible to oxidize fayalite slag at a relatively modest temperature (700<sup>o</sup> C) and to recover copper and molybdenum from the resulting hematite/silica calcine by leaching in dilute sulphuric acid. This paper addresses the considerations that need to be included in the design of a commercial scale fluidized bed operation and also discusses the potential application of fayalite slag oxidation to the recovery of base metals from copper-cobalt, copper-nickel, nickel-cobalt and pgmchrome slag. The additional challenge of separating the hematite and silica from the leached calcine to provide products with commercial potential is also examined. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

208 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Non-ferrous smelters treating copper or copper-nickel sulphide concentrates currently produce about 42 million tonnes per year of fayalite slag.  The historical accumulation was estimated by Sudbury et al. [1] at 1.2 billion tonnes adjacent to present or past smelter plants. It has been shown by Parada et al. [2] in the case of Chilean copper smelter slags that it is possible to oxidize a finely ground slag (minus 38 micron or 0.06 m<sup>2</sup> /gm), both granulated and slowly cooled, at around 700<sup>0</sup> C in an atmosphere of air plus 10% SO2 and to recover copper and molybdenum from the resulting calcine by dilute acid leaching. Commercialization of this technique requires demonstration in a pilot fluidizer operation. The role of SO2 is unclear. A set of design parameters for such a pilot operation have been developed and the some of the questions and concerns that n

eed to be addressed in the operation of the unit are discussed. The subsequent leaching of the calcine and the possible techniques for separating the hematite and silica to produce commercially acceptable products is also examined. The applicability of this technology to the reprocessing of Cu-Co, Cu-Ni-Co and PGM slag is also considered. 

### **LITERATURE SEARCH - PRIOR INVESTIGATIONS** 

References to oxidation of fayalite and/or roasting of fayalitic slag are spread diffusely through the technical literature and provide some insight into the dynamics of the oxidation process.  Pioneering work on the oxidation of relatively pure samples of synthetic fayalite was undertaken by Wones and Gilbert [3] in the 600<sup>0</sup> C to 800<sup>0</sup> C range but was limited to the formation of magnetite and silica and was focused on thermodynamic equilibria and did not explore the mineralogical process.  Gaballah, Raghy & Gleitzer [4] studied fayalite oxidation from a kinetic and morphological viewpoint, working with a synthetic single crystal of fayalite with a specific area of 0.5 m<sup>2</sup> /gm (about 4 micron diameter). The oxidation rate increased exponentially with temperature over the range 650<sup>0</sup> C to 950<sup>0</sup> C with a break at 840<sup>0</sup> C corresponding to the transformation of quartz to tridymite. Essentially complete oxidation to hematite & silica was obtained in one hour at 826<sup>o</sup> C.  The reaction rate was increased by the presence of water vapour at in a test at 777<sup>0</sup> C. The hematite grows by the formation of whiskers which then combine into plates. Mackwell [5] working with single crystals explored the rate of oxidation and concluded the rate was controlled by the rate of diffusion of iron (ions) to the iron oxide surface. Reviewing previously reported small scale test work on the oxidation of commercial slag it is noted that the work by Kimyashov et al. [6] oxidized a copper slag (40% Fe) ground to the range 7.5-40 micron (~0.06 m<sup>2</sup> /gm) in a pot achieved essentially complete oxidation to hematite of the upper half of the contents in about 6 hours at around 900<sup>o</sup> C. The lower portion was consolidated with sodium silicate migrating from the upper layer. Gyurov S. et al. [7] investigated the isothermal oxidation kinetics using 0.5 mg samples of minus 150 micron slag in a TGA apparatus on a sample of copper slag and reported reaction Oxidation was completed at 850<sup>0</sup> C in less than 30 minutes.  Reaction models were inferred from the results. Gyurov G.A. et al [8] report in European Patent 2,331,717 (August 25, 2012) oxidation of 100 gm samples of 10-30 micron size slag at 1000<sup>0</sup> C for four hours. The patent suggests a commercial 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

209 

operation could be carried out in a crucible, shaft or rotary furnace with or without a mixing operation. The aim of the roasting is to liberate the silica for subsequent reaction w

ith alkali carbonate or caustic to dissolve the silica leaving a solid residue of hematite and magnetite. Bulut G. et al. [9] describe the roasting of a copper-cobalt slag with admixture of pyrite.  The experiments were carried out on minus 100 micron mixtures of slag and pyrite in a porcelain dish in a muffle furnace. Optimum results ~ 90% cobalt solubilization in a subsequent dilute acid leach with 4:1 pyrite slag ratio at 500<sup>0</sup> C. for one hour.

### **FLUIDIZED BED POTENTIAL** 

A fluid bed operation may permit operation on coarsely granular slag (granulated or coarsely crushed), at temperatures approaching the slag liquidus (950<sup>0</sup> C – 1050<sup>0</sup> C) with good gas solid (oxygen) contact over an extended residence time (up to 8 hours).  The conceptual attractions of the fluidizer over other processing devices for slag oxidation include: 

- Little or no grinding – slag is very hard and requires 50 kWh/tonne or more to grind through 50 micron.  A 500 micron particle may be acceptable at high space velocity 1-2 metres/second, minimizing grinding cost, but this would only be acceptable only if reaction rate is high and oxygen used efficiently. 

- Operation at temperatures of incipient or transient fusion – A small amount of liquid formed on the surface of a particle when initially fed to the fluidizer may be acceptable since the products of reaction (hematite and silica have high 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

210 

melting temperatures). This will maximize reaction (diffusion) rate and/or crystal growth. 

- Long residence time – long retention time in the fluidizer can be achieved relatively inexpensively by adopting a large diameter unit with a deep (up to two metres) bed depth. This will allow time for crystal growth and may facilitate physical separation of reaction products (notably hematite and silica). The space velocity would need to be low and the fayalite feed material correspondingly fine. 

- Thermal balance – the oxidation of fayalite is slightly exothermic but will need supplementary heat to maintain a heat balance for high temperature operation (say 950<sup>o</sup> C). Fossil fuel is readily injected and combusted efficiently under oxidizing conditi

ons. - Recycling potential – the ideal products from roasting would be clean silica to recycle to the smelter as flux, a clean hematite of marketable grade and a residual siliceous glassy phase concentrating the base metals. This would reduce the cost of base metal recovery by sulphidization, sulphation or caustic treatment since the iron and silica content would be greatly reduced. No reference to the disposition of base metals in the fully oxidized slag was located. ### **PROCESS CONSIDERATIONS** ### **Volume Changes** The specific gravity of the fayalite and the reaction products are: Table 2 - Relative Volume of Reaction Products |Mineral|Mol

This might be better undertaken by transfer of hot calcine to a small separate fluidizer to permit operation at optimal SO2 concentration and temperature and minimize the volume of SO2 bearing off gas to be treated. ### **DESIGN FEATURES** Bed dimensions, bed temperature, space velocity, residence time, dust collection, feeding technique, off gas analysis, calcine quenching procedure are key design features. ### **Residence Time** The residence time required in the roaster is expected to be several hours. Higher temperatures are expected to increase iron diffusion rates and reduce residence time requirement but this could be countered by the formation of a more impermeable silica _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 216 barrier to diffusion. Coarser fayalite particle size may result in slower oxidation and screening of roaster product with grinding and recycle of oversize may be required. Clarification by investigation is needed. ### **Calcine Cooling** Two options for product cooling are dry in a fluid bed cooler and wet in a quench tank. The first would permit dry separation techniques to be applied with size reduction, if any, based on the optimum for such processing. This might permit the recovery of the majority of the silica as a high grade product by air elutriation or electrostatic separation with base metal leaching on the hematite fraction only. The second option would be quenching the roaster product with water or recycle leach solution in a quench tank. This might be favoured if a wet separation technique was effective in separating hematite and silica for example. e.g. flotation. If silica separation was feasible then the final grinding product size for the hematite would be set by the need to expose

base metal oxides to the leach solution. Prior separation of silica and could result in a lot of unnecessary grinding of silica and yield a more favorable (coarser) silica product size. ### **Calcine Equilibria** The optimal residence time for the calcine in the fluidized bed is expected to be around 6 hours. This long residence time should permit a close approach to thermodynamic equilibrium in the system. Thus the phases expected might be predicted by examination of the binary oxide systems involved notably - ### Fe2O3-SiO2-CuO-NiO-CoO-MoO3-ZnO-PbO-MgO-CaO-Al2O3 This provides a lot of permutations and combinations to be examined and at the higher temperatures the volatility of PbO, ZnO and MoO3 become significant and examination of the products from practical trials would be simpler and more informative. ### **Calcine Morphology** The crystal morphology, both the extent and direction of growth, are important in determining the physical characteristics of the roaster product. This is important since it will determine the ease of separation of silica, hematite and any residual fayalite and minor alkaline oxide phases. ### **Discussion** There are many questions that need answers before a technical and economically acceptable process for oxidizing smelter fayalite slag becomes a reality. These include the relative rates of iron ferrous ion diffusion through cast and granulated slag, the effect of operating temperature in the range 6000 C to 12000 C on oxidation rate. Higher temperature would be expected to increase ion diffusion rate which should be beneficial but will also increase the rate of silica crystal growth which could be detrimental by reducing surface product crack formation. The di

sposition of base metals in the oxidized product may also be influenced by operating temperature making them more or less available for leaching as temperature increases. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

218 

The proportion and character of the charge exiting the roaster via the flue is unclear.  It could include a slag dust portion formed in granulation or grinding, fine hematite abraded from the partially reacted slag surface as well as ash if coal is used to supply supplementary heat. Unlike sulphide roasting where high feed reaction rates can lead to local and transient super-heating and agglomeration of particles within the bed this is not expected in a slag bed. A merit of this is that wall build-up appears unlikely although a transient liquid phase may be formed above about 850<sup>0</sup> C. Thermal shock on fresh feed may lead to fracturing of feed particles. The slag if too uniform in size may result in ‘slugging’ of the bed rather than the smooth ‘bubbling’ action desired. An additional treatment step involving alkali treatment [8] or sulphation of base metals [9] or has been explored by some investigators. It does add costs and additional process compexity. 

Smelter slag is not pure ferrous silicate but includes other elements contained in the smelter feed (concentrate and flux) including oxides of commonly calcium, aluminum, and magnesium and usually at a lesser concentration oxides of titanium, chromium and alkali metals. Slags can contain mixtures of copper, nickel, cobalt and molybdenum that may respond differently to different conditions. The physical sorting of the leach residue would be targeted at a good recovery of high grade products for market. 

### **SUMMARY** 

Fayalite slag has been shown to oxidize to silica and hematite by roasting in air at temperatures between 700<sup>0</sup> C and 900<sup>0</sup> C. A conceptual design for roasting in a fluidized bed furnace at 900<sup>0</sup> C was developed for discussion purposes that would allow processing of 3.5 tonnes per day of 100 micron diameter slag per square metre of hearth (constriction plate area) with 7 hours residence time. 

Many additional questions arose in the course of this analysis that require further work to answer including the influence of slag preparation procedures, particle size and operating temperature on the kinetics of the process, the morphology of and feasibility of efficiently leaching the base metals, the solubility of calcium, magnesium and aluminum in the leach solution, the techniques required for efficiently sorting the leach residue and the marketability of the resulting silica, silicate and hematite products. 

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The concept of subjecting smelter fayalite slag to an oxidising roast is very attractive in principle as a means to recovering residual base metals from slag and separating the bulk silica, hematite and residual silicates into products with commercial potential thus increasing smelter revenue

and eliminating slag piles. Proof of concept requires expenditure of time, effort and money on further investigative work.

OF ANALYSIS** There are several technologies for arsenic removal from solution, which differ in terms of costs and the stability of the obtained residue. One of the most stable ways to dispose of an arsenic residue is by vitrification. However, it is economically unfeasible to be applied in copper production processes. Therefore, three different industrial technologies that are likely to be applied for arsenic precipitation from copper mining effluents were studied: - Scorodite precipitation: used for the treatment of high copper content solutions such as PLS from copper smelting dust leaching and effluent from copper refining processes. This process generates a stable solid which satisfies all the requirements detailed in Supreme Decree N°148. - Arsenic trisulphide: applied to generate solutions with arsenic contents below 1 ppm. The main principle involves the use of H2S gas or a NaHS solution. The final residue must be disposed of under hermetically sealed encapsulation. Also, it could be recycled to the process in order to produce a stable slag. The dissolved copper precipitates together with the arsenic. - Calcium arsenite: commonly used in effluent treatment processes. Industrially, this technique is applied for treating effluents from sulphuric acid plants which contain arsenic and traces of copper. The process consists of the addition of lime and, in some cases, the addition of ferric ions in order to ensure a low arsenic content of the final solution. The precipitated solid entraps the dissolved copper ions and generates an unstable arsenic precipitate. ### **IMMOBILISING ARSENIC WITH HIGH RATE BIOCRYSTALLISATION FOR SUSTAINABLE MINING** 

P.A. Gonzalez Contreras, M. Olde Weghuis and H. Dijkman _Paques B

.V. T. de Boerstraat 24 Balk, The Netherlands paulagonzalezcontreras@paques.nl_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

An undesirable scenario is predicted with the production of 11 million tons of arsenic from copper and lead extraction for the coming years. Paques B.V. has previously introduced the Thioteq-orpiment (As2S3) sulphide process, leading to effluents with arsenic concentrations below 0.2 mg/L. Paques has recently introduced a new arsenic immobilization process based on bio-crystallisation in airlift bioreactors: the Thioteqscorodite process. In this process, arsenic oxidation, iron oxidation and crystallisation are · mediated by microorganisms. Only scorodite (FeAsO4 2H2O) crystallisation provides a time-stable discard product to reduce the risk of arsenic leaching to the environment. Scorodite crystals contain up to 30%wt arsenic, when crystallised in the absence of gypsum. 

Currently Paques BV foresees two main applications in the copper industry: treating diluted arsenic bleed streams and processing of arsenic trioxide dust. In the Thioteq-scorodite process, a single thermophilic (70ºC) bioreactor can be used if low arsenite oxidation rates are required. However, if high arsenite oxidation rates are desired, a mesophilic (35ºC) bioreactor can be used as pre-treatment of the Thioteqscorodite reactor. Iron and neutralizing reagents can be chosen to minimize gypsum production, depending of the geographical location of the mine site, leading the arsenic immobilization process to a new sustainable concept. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

232 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Arsenic use is banned for most applications and as consequence it has accumulated as mainly arsenic trioxide (As2O3), a very soluble form of arsenic (20 g/L) [1]. Arsenic trioxide powder has been stored until suitable technologies for its safe disposal are developed. An example of arsenic trioxide storage underground is at the Giant Mine (Yellowknife, Canada) with the dumping of 260,000 tons of roaster dust [2]. There is not a market for arsenic trioxide and therefore arsenic waste conversion to a time-stable discard product is essential. To the best of our knowledge only scorodite (FeAsO4·2H2O), a stable mineral, fits that requirement. 

In the last decade, the processing of ores containing arsenic has slowly raised interest on arsenic removal and its immobilization. Worldwide, several research groups have focused in the thermophilic bioleaching of chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) [3] and enargite (Cu3AsS4) [4] and bio-oxidation of arsenopyrite (FeAsS) [5].Their results have shown that bioleaching rates can be improved, resulting even in higher copper recovery yield than chemical leaching of the same minerals. However, bacterial inhibition due to the release of arsenic from those minerals have been observed [5]. 

The interest in copper and gold refractory ores containing arsenic is highly illustrated by the number of studies conducted during the last years. Scorodite crystals have a

lso been precipitated at atmospheric temperatures (~90 º C) by chemical precipitation and gypsum addition, which has been extensively studied in the last 20 years by several researches [6, 7]. 

Scorodite mineral is recognized by researchers and mining companies as the safest and logical option to stabilize arsenic for long term storage. However, the high costs associated to chemical precipitation, compared to bio-crystallisation, have delayed the arsenic immobilization and many companies have chosen for the arsenic precipitation at mesophilic temperatures leading to arsenic-ferrihydrite precipitates. 

In 2003 Paques has patented a bioprocess to crystallise arsenic into scorodite: the Thioteq-scorodite process, also named the bioscorodite process. From 2008 to 2012, the bioscorodite process was developed with the aid of Wageningen University. Nowadays, bio-crystallisation of scorodite at 70 º C in a continuous operating airlift bio-reactor is a very successful process. Currently, the Thioteq-scorodite process is based on biological iron oxidation and arsenate. Paques is assessing to enhance the process by incorporating the biological arsenite oxidation, minimising the gypsum production and optimising the reactor design for bio-crystallisation and biological oxidation processes. 

In this paper, the state of the art of the Thioteq-scorodite process is presented and the required steps to optimise the process are discussed.

### **ARSENIC BIO-CRYSTALLISATION AND THE THIOTEQ-SCORODITE PROCESS** 

Paques has demonstrated the Thioteq-technology with several precipitation processes such as copper sulphide, zinc sulphide and nickel sulphide. A large scale installation based on Thioteq technology is commissioned at a goldmine in the Americas where over 10 tons per day of copper are recovered as copper sulphide from effluents that would otherwise have been precipitated together with gypsum and send to the tailings dam. 

One of the latest implementations of the Thioteq-technology is arsenic recovery and its immobilisation. Paques has introduced two new bioprocesses for arsenic removal: orpiment (As2S3) and scorodite (FeAsO4·2H2O) crystallisation. In the Thioteq-orpiment process, arsenic oxide reacts with sulphide to form 3- orpiment that has a very low solubility under anoxic conditions. Arsenate (AsO4 ) is first 3- reduced by sulphide to arsenite (AsO3 ) and subsequently crystallised as orpiment at acidic conditions (pH < 3). Advantages of orpiment are its compact volume and its high arsenic content with 61% mass arsenic and no crystal water [8]. In the chemical step of the Thioteq-orpiment process the metal sulphide precipitation takes place; and in the biological step sulphide is produced and transported to the chemical precipitation stage with a recycled carried gas [8]. Despite the low solubility of orpiment at anoxic conditions, it can release arsenite into solution if stored under aerobic condit

ions. Orpiment oxidation tends to increase at pH>8 and in the presence of oxidizing reagents such as manganese or ferric iron [9]. Besides, under low oxygen conditions, carbonates may also dissolve orpiment. Therefore orpiment should be deposited in a (semi) closed landfill to avoid infiltration of oxygen and or carbonate rich water. 

The Thioteq-scorodite process is a new sustainable Paques-solution to arsenic removal and its immobilisation. In the Thioteq-scorodite process, air is used to oxidise iron and arsenic by specialised microorganisms. In this process, one compact air-lift loop bioreactor (Circox®–technology) is the core of the production of arsenic-containing crystals, i.e. bioscorodite crystals for safe and long term disposal of arsenic. 

### **THE THIOTEQ-SCORODITE PROCESS** 

The Thioteq™-scorodite process is a proven technology patented and developed by Paques B.V. The invention of the Thioteq-scorodite process involves arsenic removal and its immobilisation into bio-crystals. This innovative process explores the use of oxidising microorganisms at pH between 0.5 and 4 and at temperatures between 20 and 90 º C. 

In general, the operational costs of the Thioteq-scorodite process are lower when compared to chemical precipitation. Some features that reduce operational costs are: 

- i- biological oxidation and crystallisation reactions occur in one reactor (for diluted streams), 

- ii- air is used as oxidant instead of chemical oxidants such oxygen or hydrogen peroxide,

### **Biological arsenic oxidation** 

The Thioteq-scorodite process has been tested at laboratory scale (10 L) for simultaneous biological iron and arsenite oxidation at 70ºC and pH 1.2 [13]. Similar results were also obtained by external researchers [14]. The measured arsenite oxidation rates at 70ºC were five times lower than the concomitant iron oxidation rates and therefore only diluted arsenite streams (< 1 g As<sup>3+</sup> /L) can be treated. These results have been presented at the IBS 2013 conference by Gonzalez _et al_ . [5]. 

Paques B.V. has an alternative bio-process to deal with high arsenite concentrations such as during the processing of arsenic trioxide (As2O3). Biological arsenite oxidation can reduce the costs related to oxidant reagent consumption such as hydrogen peroxide and extra reactors for arsenic oxidation. Furthermore, biological arsenite oxidation occurs at high rates in mesophilic conditions (30-40ºC). Paques is currently testing biological arsenite oxidation in the Thioteq-scorodite process at 30ºC. The outcome of those experiments will be presented in this conference. 

### **Minimizing gypsum production** 

Acid generation in precipitation reactor is controlled by adding neutralizing reagents such as limestone (CaCO3) or lime (Ca(OH)2). The addition of neutralizing · reagents containing calcium will lead to the formation of gypsum (CaSO4 2H2O) (Equation 1a). In the chemical precipitation of scorodite, iron chemical oxidation, arsenic chemical oxidation and precipitation are each conducted in a separated reactor at 90ºC. Ferric iron, arsenate and limestone (or lime) are mixed in the precipitation reactor, leading to the formation of gypsum an

d scorodite. Then more than half of the solids are gypsum precipitates, leading to an inferior scorodite product with ~10-15% wt. As.

A proton neutral scorodite precipitation reaction can be achieved if an alternative iron source is used such as scrap iron. The protons released during arsenite biological oxidation and scorodite precipitation are neutralised by the protons consumed during the scrap iron oxidation to ferric iron. 

Depending of the geographical location of mine sites, iron and neutralising reagents can be chosen to minimise gypsum production and increase the arsenic content in the residue. A decrease in gypsum production results in lower post-treatment costs related to dewatering, filtering and sludge disposal. Alternative iron-carbonate mineral sources can be found at different locations. 

### **Circox reactor to enhance crystallization reactions** 

The CIRCOX® (CIRCulation OXydation reactor) technology is a compact aerobic biological reactor for the treatment of wastewater.

Figure 4 is a schematic diagram of a Circox® airlift reactor. The cylindrical reactor contains another cylinder, which divides the reactor into two compartments. 

The outside compartment functions as a riser, where air is introduced (3). The inside compartment functions as a downer (5). Because of the air hold-up in the riser (9), the density of the suspension (crystal/wastewater mixture) in the riser is lower compared to the density of the suspension in the downer. This density difference results in an up going flow in the riser and a down going flow in the downer. Therefore the suspension is circulated around the central cylinder. This circulation flow is the primary airlift flow. This relatively high liquid flow (~1 m/s) results in a well-mixed reactor system, in which the crystals and biomass are easily kept in suspension. 

The influent is brought into the downer (1). The air leaves the reactor system at the top of the reactor (4). A special designed Circoxseparator at top of the reactor (11-15) separates the treated wastewater from the crystals. The treated wastewater lea

### **SULPHIDE PRECIPITATION AS A NOVEL APPROACH TO REMOVE ARSENIC FROM COPPER SMELTER SCRUBBER EFFLUENT** 

P. Littlejohn, A. Hall and D. Kratochvil _BioteQ Environmental Technologies Suite 1000-1050 West Pender Street Vancouver, Canada V6E 3S7 plittlejohn@bioteq.ca_

### **ABSTRACT** 

Many new copper deposits being developed contain elevated levels of arsenic, leading to a trend of increasing arsenic content in copper concentrates traded and processed globally. Smelting of these high arsenic concentrates generates high levels of dissolved arsenic in gas scrubber effluents, which must be removed before the wastewater can be discharged or re-used. Typical treatment approach involves lime neutralization, often with ferric iron addition, to remove arsenic in the form of insoluble calcium and ferric arsenates. This approach results in the production of large quantities of sludge which must be stabilized prior to final disposal, increasing treatment costs. This paper provides an overview of sulphide precipitation as an alternate process for selective removal of arsenic and dissolved metals from scrubber effluent at copper smelters. Results from recent test work completed using BioteQ’s BioSulphide process technology to treat two scrubber effluent streams are presented. Scrubber purge streams containing arsenic concentrations of > 7 g/L were effectively treated to < 0.3 mg/L final arsenic content, producing arsenic free weak acid for recycle and re-use in the smelter process while reducing the quantity of waste solids generated. Process options for concurrent recovery of dissolved copper and other valuable metals such as rhenium from scrubber effluent were also found to be possible with sulphide precipitation combined with selective ion exchange.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Arsenic management is a growing issue in the copper industry. When arsen

ic bearing copper sulphide minerals is smelted, arsenic bearing SOx gas is generated. This gas is treated with scrubbers prior to discharge, generating scrubber liquor high in arsenic, sulphuric acid, and other metals. In Latin America this scrubber liquor is known as EPAS - _Efluente Planta Acido Sulfurico_ . In order for smelter scrubber effluent to be discharged or re-used, arsenic must be removed from the solution. Several classes of treatment options for arsenic exist, including precipitation, adsorption, ion exchange, reverse osmosis and cementation. For solutions such as EPAS that contain high dissolved arsenic, free acid and a host of other heavy metals, precipitation processes are the most common method of arsenic management [1]. When EPAS solution is treated with lime and air, the first reaction that occurs is the neutralization of sulphuric acid to produce gypsum (Equation 1). Arsenic is typically in the As(III) form in EPAS rather than the As(V) form, so the second reaction is the oxidation of arsenic (Equation 2). Following this, calcium arsenate is formed (Equation 3) [2]. 







Calcium arsenate is relatively unstable and is classed as hazardous waste due to high release of arsenic during TCLP testing. Additionally, lime treatment of arsenic is not typically able to reach low enough concentrations of arsenic in solution for safe discharge. As a result, pure lime precipitation of arsenic is less common than in decades past. In order to produce stable sludge, lime treatment is supplemented with iron addition in order to co-precipitate iron and arsenic as arsenical ferrihydrite. The stability of such arsenical ferrihydrite increases as the ratio of iron to arsenic exceeds 3:1. Lime is necessary to remove free acid and increase the pH to 4-9, at which point arsenical ferrihydrite forms as per Equation 4 [3]. 



While the resultant sludge is stable provided the appropriate dosage of iron and lime is used, the sludge produced is high volume and contains significant moisture. This in turn can complicate the water balance of the overall process, particularly in dry 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

245 

climates or at sites with limited fresh water accessibility where water recycle is necessary. 

An alternative to iron stabilized precipitation of arsenic with lime is sulphidization of EPAS to produce sulphide solids. In this process, sulphide is added to the feed liquor to precipitate metals as high grade sulphide solids. Sulphide may be added to solution in a variety of forms. In this paper the sulphide source is hydrogen sulphide gas or dissolved calcium hydrosulphide. The reaction chemistry for the sulphidization of arsenic is shown below (Equations 5 and 6). Arsenic in the EPAS is in the reduced As(III) form and thus no extra sulphide is necessary to reduce it from the As(V) form prior to precipitation, unlike high ORP liquor. 





Copper sulphidization is shown in Equation 7. It is worth noting that sulphidization

of copper results in an increase in solution acidity, while sulphidization of arsenic does not produce acid. 



Metals such as arsenic and copper are relatively insoluble in the presence of sulphide, even at the low pH found in EPAS liquor. As a result, neutralization of free acid prior to metal precipitation is unnecessary which avoids the generation of gypsum solids, and the volume of sludge produced is a fraction of that produced when lime is used. The arsenic free acid can often be re-used such that the value of acid and water contained in the treated EPAS stream is recovered. Additionally, metal sulphide solids have a higher specific gravity than gypsum/lime sludge, leading to better settling/filterability and higher overall water recovery. In this paper the results of two laboratory programs will be discussed in the context of arsenic sludge, water balance, and overall metal recovery.

### **ABSTRACT** 

In order to selectively recover copper (Cu) and zinc (Zn) over iron (Fe) from acid mine drainage (AMD)generated from one abandoned copper mine located in east Japan, the feasibility of integrating lime neutralization treatment with sodium hydrosulfide (NaHS) sulfidization was investigated. At first, lime neutralization was applied to the AMD to find the precipitation behaviors of Cu, Zn and Fe. Next, NaHS sulfidization as well as the integration with lime neutralization were conducted to separately precipitate Cu, Zn, and Fe from the AMD. The results showed that by lime neutralization treatment, all of the Fe precipitated at pH 5, whereas Cu and Zn precipitated at pH 6-8. After Fe was fully precipitated by lime at pH 5, it was also capable of selectively precipitating Cu over Zn by adding 10-15 mg/L NaHS. Finally, Zn could be precipitated by lime neutralization to above pH 9 after Cu and Fe were precipitated. Based on the results, a modified alternative treatment approach for separately recovering Cu and Zn over Fe from the AMD was proposed.
