### **INTRODUCTION** 

Acid mine drainage (AMD) generated from a metal mine contains a broad range of heavy metals which have adverse effects on aquatic life and human beings [1-2]. Generally, AMD is treated by neutralization method such as lime neutralization or limestone neutralization to remove the heavy metals by forming their insoluble hydroxide precipitates [3-4]. Although neutralization is an effective method for AMD treatment, it is also accompanied by the treatment of produced metal hydroxide precipitate, which has costly disposal requirements. 

One abandoned copper mine, located in east Japan, discharges about 12 m<sup>3</sup> /min of AMD from several galleries and pits, which is gathered and treated in the downstream purification plant. The main heavy metals contained in the AMD are copper (Cu), zinc (Zn), and iron (Fe).The present treatment process is by lime neutralization, where lime slurry is introduced to adjust the pH of AMD to about pH 10 to precipitate all of the heavy metals. After solid-liquid separation by gravitation sedimentation, sulfuric acid (H2SO4) is introduced to adjust the pH of the AMD to about pH 7. All of the heavy metals’ concentrations in the effluent can meet the Japanese effluent standards. The precipitate generated in the neutralization process is pumped to a landfill disposal site. Owing to the decrease in the capacity of landfill disposal site as well as the increase in the price of base metals such as Cu in recent years, it is expected that not only to treat but also to recover these base metals from the AMD. For the subsequent Cu and Zn smelting process, it is needed to selectively precipitate Cu and Zn over Fe from the AMD. 

In this study, we want to achieve this objective by integrating the present lime neutralization treatment process with NaHS sulfidization. At first, lime neutralization was applied to the AMD to find the precipitation behavior of Cu, Zn, and Fe. Next, NaHS sulfidization as well as the integration with lime neutralization were conducted to separately precipitate Cu, Zn, and Fe from the AMD. Finally, a modified alternative approach for the AMD treatment was proposed based on the optimal conditions obtained from the above results. A consecutive experiment of the proposed approach was also carried out for the AMD. The effectiveness was evaluated by analyzing the concentration of Cu, Zn, and Fe in the effluents, as well as the content of Cu, Zn, and Fe in the precipitates generated at each treatment stage.

### **Methods** 

All experiments were carried out by batch experiment at room temperature (i.e. at about 293 K). In each experiment, 200 mL of AMD was poured into a 300 mL beaker equipped with a stainless magnetic stirrer. After the addition of reagent, the liquid was mixed at 400 rad/min. The neutralization experiment was conducted by introducing lime powder (particle size below 75 µm) into the beaker to adjust the pH of the AMD. In the sulfidization experiment, 10 g/L of NaHS solution was freshly prepared beforehand. The needed volume of the NaHS solution was introduced into the AMD whose pH had been previously adjusted by lime. When the desired pH in the neutralization experiment was reached or the sulfidization experiment was completed, 5 mL of liquid was sampled and filtered through a 0.2 µm membrane filter for analysis. The concentrations of Cu, Zn, and Fe in the sampled liquid were analyzed with an ICP-OES (Inductively Coupled Plasma - Optical Emission Spectrometer, Perkin Elmer, Optima 5300). 

In the consecutive experiment, the integrated approach including multiple treatment stages based on the optimal conditions obtained from the lime neutralization and NaHS sulfidization experiments were applied to 5 L of AMD. Solid-liquid separation was performed by using vacuum filtration after each treatment stage. The liquid fraction (AMD) was sampled for metal concentration analysis with the ICP-OES before being moved to the next treatment stage. The solid fraction (precipitate) was dried, weighed, and the metal contents were analyzed with the ICP-OES after being dissolved by aqua regia.

### **ZINC IN THE COPPER SECONDARY PRODUCTION AND POTENTIAL RECYCLING TECHNOLOGIES** 

R. Rumpold and J. Antrekowitsch _Christian Doppler Laboratory for Optimization and Biomass Utilization in Heavy Metal Recycling Franz-Josef-Str. 18 8700 Leoben, Austria rene.rumpold@unileoben.ac.at_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Zinc enters the copper production cycles as an appreciable amount of raw materials contain zinc, especially the secondary ones. Based on its characteristics and the process parameters during the copper production, the zinc is evaporated and concentrated in the flue dust. The content of that metal in such dusts can be up to 45 %, therefore they represent a valuable secondary zinc source. Unfortunately it is not possible to use them directly in the primary zinc metallurgy, because of high halogen concentrations, which are disturbing the electrowinning process of zinc. Moreover the presence of high lead-, tin- and copper-concentrations results in higher efforts to recycle them by that process route. Therefore separate recycling technologies have to be used to extract the valuable metal fraction from those residues. The variety of potential processes is quite high as hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical principles can be used as well as both combined. This work gives an overview about the behavior of zinc in the copper secondary metallurgy and it shows strategies to recycle the valuable fraction from evolving dusts.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper represents the third most important metal in quantity after iron and aluminum, based on an annual production of 19 million metric tons. About 17.5 % of the copper is recovered by recycling secondary materials [1]. In principle the secondary production can be divided in a melting and reducing step followed by converting and refining. These pyrometallurgical processes are used to remove impurities, which enter through secondary materials like scrap or slags. Because of the constantly rising requirement of sustainable production and to cover the steadily increasing demand, low grade materials are processed. These materials are partly contaminated with significant amounts of undesirable elements, which have to be removed to recover pure copper. 

Zinc represents a major impurity in the copper recycling, as it is often used in copper alloys like brass. Therefore, it can be found in residue

s of the copper secondary industry, which in turn can be used as secondary zinc source. This study shows the behavior of zinc within the copper processing as well as potential recycling technologies for generated zinc containing residues. 

### **SECONDARY COPPER PRODUCTION** 

The secondary copper industry processes a wide range of different raw materials. Therefore, the next paragraphs give an overview about the raw materials and the individual processing steps for them. 

### **Raw materials for copper recycling** 

The secondary raw materials can be divided in two major groups, metallic and oxidic fraction. In general, the copper recycling uses a wide range of copper containing materials like low grade material with copper contents of only 2 % as well as high grade material up to 99 %. According to table 1, nearly all secondary copper materials can contain zinc, except high grade copper scrap. Cable- or home scraps are typical examples for this kind of raw material. The contamination of this source is generally low and in the most cases limited to organic substances, like insulation material from cable scrap. [2, 3] 

One of the most important copper containing recycling sources is the copper alloy scrap. The range of different copper based alloys is very wide and nearly all of them contain zinc. Brass and bronze are the most common representatives of this group. Beside zinc also a number of further metals like lead, tin, nickel etc. are included. Usually these materials are only remelted to generate alloys again by adding the necessary elements. Nevertheless, copper alloy scrap is very often processed in the secondary copper production and therefore the mentioned elements enter the copper production cycle. [2, 3] 

Another raw material for copper recycling from brass and bronze industry are the slags and drosses, which are generated during the fabrication of the alloys. In contrast to the scraps, these secondary sources are oxidic and therefore, they have to be processed within the copper recycling. Also drosses from other metal industries (e.g. lead refining) are processed in this way. [2, 3] 

A relatively new raw material for copper recycling is electronic scrap. In addition to the copper precious metals are included, which can be recovered as by-product in electrolysis. But also significant tin and zinc amounts can be found, because of the used soldering joints. The metallic fraction is accompanied by an organic fraction which is hard to remove, therefore, new process systems are designed to handle such contaminations re

spectively to use them as process agent (e.g. for heating). [2-6] 

During the processing of copper, the contaminants are removed through different phases, like slags or dusts. In most cases this process residues contain high copper amounts (converter, anode furnace slag) and have to be recycled or processed internally. Therefore these materials represent a main raw material, especially for the reduction step. [6, 7] 

Copper and also copper alloys are common plating metals for decorative as well as engineering purposes. The deposition of the desired coating can be produced chemically or electrochemically, whereby the last method dominates. This procedure leads to copper containing residues like sludges. Another source of secondary copper materials like this are sludges from hydrometallurgical refining (e.g. cementation in the zinc refining). As shown in table 1 these sludges can contain very high zinc amounts up to 20 %. [6, 8]

This flow sheet presents the typical material flows during the copper recycling, whereby a strong dependency of the input material is given. As mentioned above the secondary copper industry processes a wide range of raw materials with increasingly complex character. Therefore the secondary raw materials are

### <u>Smelting and Reduction</u> 

The first step of the copper recycling processes low grade material. This fraction consists of oxidic and heavy contaminated copper bearing substances, like slags, sludges, dusts, electronic scrap etc. Because of the presence of nonmetallic copper, the charge has to be reduced in addition to the smelting. Today modern batch reactors are continuously replacing old technologies, like shaft or electric furnaces. Especially the increasingly complex residues, like electronic scrap need more flexible aggregates. The AUSMELT/ISASMELT technologies are able to fulfill these requirements as well as a Top Blown Rotary Converter (TBRC). Figure 1 shows that the smelting and reduction step uses also the slag from the subsequent processes to recover the contained copper. [68]

### <u>Converting</u> 

The black copper (~80 % Cu) produced in the first step is further processed in the converter. In this reactor oxygen is used to remove the metallic impurities like iron, l

ead, tin, zinc, etc., which origin on the one hand from the reduction step and on the other hand from the additionally charged old- and alloy scraps. In the most cases the traditional Peirce Smith converter is used for this purpose, whereby also TBRC´s are suited in for that treatment. The slag of the converting process contains a large amount of copper and therefore, has to be recirculated to the reduction step. Another option is to treat the slag in a lead/tin reduction furnace if the adjacent amounts are high enough. [6, 7] 

### <u>Fire Refining</u> 

The last pyrometallurgical process in the copper recycling is the fire refining in an anode furnace. Converter copper with a copper content of ~96 % is upgraded by a further oxidation with a subsequently reduction to anode copper with a purity of 98 %. The slag is returned to the first step. Beside copper from converting, high grade scraps and anode residues from the electrolysis are added. [6, 7]

Based on the high zinc amount in nearly every raw material this element represents a major impurity in copper recycling. The thermochemical characteristics of relatively high vapor pressure and low Gibbs free energy of the oxide allow an easy removal via slag or flue dust. ### **RECYCLING OF ZINC RICH FLUE DUST** 

The behavior of zinc shows that it is mainly discharged through flue dusts and partly via the slag of the smelting and reduction step. The slag is granulated and used as construction material, therefore, the contained zinc is lost. In contrast, the flue dust contains a number of commercial metals like zinc, tin, lead and copper, which justify its recycling. Based on the high zinc content of such materials it could be a high grade material for the zinc production, especially as this industry allows the additional recovery of the further included valuable metals. Nevertheless, these secondary sources cannot be processed directly as they contain high amounts up to 10 % of the halogens fluorine, chlorine and bromine. These elements enter the copper recycling mainly through plastics from electronic scrap (include ~20 % organics) etc. and leave it through the flue dust, as easily volatile compounds. [3, 4, 6, 10, 11, 12] 

The primary zinc production, in particular the electrowinning process, is very sensitive against chlorine and fluorine, as hydrofluoric- and hydrochloric acid is generated. These substances lead to the dissolution of the lead anode on the one hand and to the destruction of the aluminum oxide layer of the cathode on the other hand. Moreover the chlorine in the solution leads to chlorine gas formation at the anode, which causes safety risks. Therefore, the maximum halogen concentrations in the zinc elect

rolysis are limited to 100 mg/l Cl and 50 mg/l F. 

In principle the halogens can be removed from residues by thermal or hydrometallurgical methods, but the common halogen removal processes don’t reach the required low levels for secondary copper dusts with an economic effort. Consequently, this material needs separate processes for the valuable metal recovery. [13] 

The recycling of secondary copper flue dusts allows hydrometallurgical as well as pyrometallurgical processes. 

### **Hydrometallurgical processing of secondary copper dust** 

The hydrometallurgical methods offer numerous options to recover the valuable metals. In principle they are leached completely or partly followed by a selective extraction. Figure 6 sums up the common recycling techniques separated in the associated process steps. Very often a halogen removal is carried out previous to the shown treatments, as moderate to low values can be achieved by simple water or soda dissolution. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

273 



Figure 6 – Hydrometallurgical recycling techniques [12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18] 

The conventional technology for the recycling of secondary copper dusts is leaching with sulfuric acid followed by cementation and finally crystallization of zincsulfate. Lead and tin are not soluble at these conditions and can be separated by filtration. The lead and tin rich filter cake can be further processed in the lead industry. In the next step copper is removed from the solution by cementation. Therefore, iron scrap or zinc are representing potential cementation agents. The advantage of zinc is that no iron is added in the process. When iron is already present in the solution, scrap can be used as cementation agent, as it is cheaper and has to be removed anyway. Finally the zinc is recovered by crystallization of zinc-sulfate. [12, 14] 

Another, relatively similar approach is to separate the zinc selectively via solvent extraction from the solution and to recover it by electrolysis. This technology is known as Zincex process, but due to the risk of a chlorine and organic contamination of the electrolyte it is not widely applied yet. [12, 14, 16] 

Beside the typical sulfuric acid based processes, also ammonia can be used to recover valuable metals. The EZINEX process represents the most common method using this medium. Thereby ammonia chloride is used to dissolve the heavy metal fraction (except iron) followed by solution purification via cementation with zinc. In the end the pure zinc is recovered by a novel electrolysis, which represents the core of the EZINEX technology. Instead of the sulfate system, which is usually used in the zinc industry, a chloride based electrolysis is applied. The presence of NH3 eliminates harmful chlorine and the used graphite anode is resistant again hydrochloric acid. Furthermore the fluorine sensitiveness is also low, because of the Ca<sup>2+</sup> presence (formation of CaF2) and the used titanium cathodes. [12, 14, 17

] 

The leaching of metal oxides in the NH3-(NH4)2CO3 is an alternative ammonium treatment, but due to the interference of chlorides, a halogen removal in advance is necessary. After the solution purification by cementation zinc carbonate can be precipitated. [12, 14] 

A relatively new method is given by the so called FLUREC process. It leaches the heavy metal fraction with a hydrochloric acid containing solution. The subsequent cementation removes lead, copper etc. and enables a selective solvent extraction. After 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

274 

re-extracting the zinc into a sulfuric acid solution, high purity zinc can be recovered by conventional electrolysis. [14, 15] 

The leaching with caustic soda enables a selective dissolution of lead and zinc, whereas the lead is cementated by zinc to purify the solution in the subsequent step. Finally the pure zinc is recovered by electrolysis. Based on filtration problems, limited dissolution of zinc-ferrite and the necessary advanced halogen removal, this process is not really appropriate for treating secondary copper dusts. 

### **Pyrometallurgical processing of secondary copper dust** 

The pyrometallurgical processes are only rarely used for the copper dust recycling. The available process reduces the contained metal compounds. Furthermore soda is added to bind sulfur in the slag. High temperatures lead to a zinc concentration in the flue dust. Remaining lead and tin form a marketable alloy. In fact only high tin and lead contents in combination with low halogen concentrations justify such a processing, therefore, this process is not suitable for modern secondary copper dusts. [12, 19] 

### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

The “Christian Doppler Laboratory for Optimization and Biomass Utilization in Heavy Metal Recycling” is working on the recycling of heavy metal containing flue dusts. Recovering valuable metals from copper secondary dust represents one major field of investigation in that context. Today these dusts are sold to external recycler and the valuable metal content (especially copper and tin) of this material is lost. Therefore, aim of this research is to design a process which allows a convenient internal recycling. Consequently two potential pyro- and hydrometallurgical methods are investigated. The main focus of this research lays on the simultaneous recovery of the valuable metals and not only zinc. Especially, as the value of other contained metals could be higher. 

### **Pyrometallurgical process** 

The pyrometallurgical process is based on the high vapor pressure of metallic zinc at elevated temperatures (Figure 2a). Consequently the aim is to concentrate it by vaporization and following oxidation/condensation. Figure 7 shows a possible flow sheet of the pyrometallurgical treatment. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

275 



Figure – 7 Flow sheet of pyrometallurgical copper dust recycling 

The first step is the removal of halogens as complete as possi

ble by a soda leaching. On the one hand the low halogen content in the feed leads to higher crude zinc oxide quality and on the other hand to halogen rich solutions, which are suitable for bromine production. The core process of this method is the reduction of agglomerated dust by an iron enriched copper bath. Iron acts as reducing agent for lead, copper and tin, which are collected in the copper. Zinc oxide is also reduced and separated by vaporization. Finally a copper alloy with mainly lead, tin, zinc and iron as well as crude zinc oxide is produced. The alloy can be returned to the converting step or to the slag reduction (see figure 1). The crude zinc oxide can be soda leached again to increase the quality or it can be sold directly. Beside the copper alloy and the zinc oxide also a slag occurs, which can be granulated and presents a potential material for road construction. 

The first trials were carried out in a natural gas heated crucible with a material input sum of approximately 15 kg. Additionally, some larger scale trials in a Top Blown Rotary Converter (TBRC), with a material input of 100 kg being prepared. Figure 8 shows the TBRC for the mentioned experiments. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

276 









Figure 8 – Top blown rotary converter 

The first results of the small scale trials showed, that it is possible to separate the valuable metals according to the flow sheet. 99 % of the tin and >92 % of copper can be collected in the metal bath. Nearly 75 % of the zinc is evaporated and finally recovered in the dust. The lead distribution shows 70 % in the metal and 30 % in the dust. 

### **Hydrometallurgical process** 

Another experimental series is focused on the hydrometallurgical recovering of the valuable metals. The first step again is the soda leaching, which allows the production of bromine. Afterwards the flue dust is leached with sulfuric acid to dissolve zinc and copper, while lead and tin stay in the residue. In principle two strategies can be pursued, on the one hand the leaching with low and on the other hand with high sulfuric acid concentrations. The first case leads to high zinc and moderate copper contents in the solution, while the stronger conditions result in higher copper and zinc dissolution. Lead and tin are concentrated in the filter cake and can be recycled in the converting step of the secondary processing. After leaching, the liquor is purified by cementation with zinc. Copper, but also lead and tin (very small amounts are also leached) are removed by the addition of zinc powder. This process leads to a copper cementate, which can be returned to the converter or the anode furnace, depending on the purity. Finally the relatively clean zinc solution can be used as potential raw material for a zinc sulfate production. This process represents a separate field of research in the Christian Doppler Laboratory carried out by Steinlechner [19, 20] and is therefore not discussed in detail.

The first results showed quite satisfactory results, as the weak leaching conditions with 0.25 M H2SO4 lead to dissolution rates of 92 % zinc, 20 % copper, 0.2 % lead and 0.15 % tin. In contrast the strong conditions with 2 M H2SO4 result in 99 % zinc, 75 % copper 0.13 % lead and 0.5 % tin leaching. That means, the cementation effort in the second case is higher, but in return nearly the whole zinc can be extracted by higher sulfuric acid additions. 

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The increasingly complex secondary raw materials for the copper recycling lead to high foreign metal input. These metals are selectively removed in various process steps, whereby process residues like slags, sludges or flue dust are generated. While the slags (lead and tin) and sludges (precious metals) are processed internally, the zinc rich flue dusts are often sold to external recycler. Therefore, the contained valuable metal fraction is lost, but especially if slag treatment furnaces are available, the internal recycling would make sense. In that context, this paper shows the behavior of the major 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

278 

impurity, zinc and a pyro- as well as a hydrometallurgical method for internal recycling. Both techniques use a soda leaching step, not only to remove the halogens, but rather to produce a halogen rich solution, that’s bromine content allows an economic recycling. Furthermore, the gained solution can be easily enriched if waste heat from pyrometallurgical recycling processes is used to evaporate water from the liquor. Therefore, the bromine concentration can be adjusted to get the maximum value. 

The pyrometallurgical process shows satisfying results as 99 % tin and 92 % copper are recovered via the alloy. This can be seen very positive as nearly the whole fraction of the main metal in value can be recycled. On the other hand only 75 % of the zinc is evaporated, which means that 25 % are returned and circulated in the copper recycling. But also the lead distribution is not really acceptable as 30 % were found in the flue dust. That means on the one hand, lead was not recovered completely and on the other hand it contaminates the crude zinc oxide. Particularly the second impact is negative, as the crude zinc oxide has to be further processed and cannot be sold directly. 

The weak leaching with sulfuric acid results in a high lead and tin recovery as only 0.2 % lead and 0.15 % tin are dissolved. Consequently, the concentrated filter cake can be directly returned to the converting step. Especially, as 80 % of the copper are also remain in this leaching residue. The residual 20 % can be easily removed by cementation and are also returned to the converter. The leaching efficiency for zinc is about 92 % that means 8 % would be circulated. Another approach uses more acidic conditions, which results in nearly complete zinc di

ssolution. But this leads also to a higher copper and a significant tin amount in the solution, which in turn causes a higher cementation effort. Therefore the weak conditions will be recommended as the zinc in the filter cake is not lost, it is only returned to the copper recycling process. 

To sum up the carried out investigations, it could be seen that both processes work in general. The reducing process offer high recovery rates for copper and tin, while the leaching allows an optimal recycling for the whole valuable metal fraction. Furthermore an economic point of view prefers the hydrometallurgical process, as the pyrometallurgical treatment requires a metal bath at high temperatures.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The Pb/Sn solder has been used as interconnecting materials, but the solder has been substituted by Pb-free solder due to toxicity of Pb. There is an increasing concern about treating the Pb-free solder generated in electric home appliance industry. The recycling process of Pb-free solder containing Sn-Ag-Cu as main components was developed using stannic chloride solution. The leaching behaviors of Sn, Ag, Cu were investigated under the leaching conditions; stannic concentration, 0.2 mol/L; stirring speed, 200 rpm - 600 rpm; pulp density, 1.0%; temperature, 30 °C – 90 °C. HCl concentration, 0.5 mol/L – 3.0 mol/L. Tin was dissolved within 15 min because stannic ion could oxidize selectively tin but not silver. The leaching efficiency of tin increased to more than 99% under the leaching condition; SnCl4 concentraion, 0.2 mol/L; HCl concentration, 1mol/L; pulp density, 1%; temperature, 50 °C; stirring speed, 400 rpm. Though copper metal is not oxidized by stannic ion, some of Cu dissolved in HCl solution. Therefore, copper ion was removed from the leachate by adding tin powder. The copper was not detected by cementation adding tin powder under the following conditions; amount of tin, 1 %; temperature 50 °C and stirring speed 400 rpm. This result indicates that tin could be selectively recovered successfully from waste Pb-free solder.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

In EU, WEEE (the Waste of Electrical and Electronic Equipment) and RoHS (the Restriction of the use of certain Hazardous Substances) prevent using lead (Pb) in electrical and electronic equipments due to its toxicity [1-2],

and, in many countries, governments have tried to regulate the use of lead. Lead-free solder has been predominant by substituting the tin/lead solder, and many kinds of Pb-free solder series have been developed using tin, silver, copper, bismuth, antimony, and zinc [3]. Melting processes have been representative processes to reuse waste Pb-free solder [4]. There are increasing concerns about hazardous gas emission generated from combustion of organic flux in the Pb-free solder [4]. 

Hydrometallurgical routes are alternative processes to recycle the waste Pb-free solder. Rhee et al. [5] performed the feasibility study on Sn recovery from lead frame scrap using sodium hydroxide with sodium persulfate as an oxidant. Kim et al. [6] investigated the leaching behavior of tin in NaOH solution to recover tin from waste Pbfree solder. There have been a few studies on the recycling of waste Pb-free solder under the acidic condition although nitric acid leaching tests were performed to recover valuable metals from waste Pb-free solder [4] and printed circuit boards [7]

In the previous study [4], HNO3 leaching was presented to recover tin, silver, and copper from waste Pb-free solder as shown in Fig. 1. Silver and copper are dissolved by

nitric acid leaching while tin component precipitates as stannic acid. In the present study, a new recycling process using stannic chloride solution was investigated to avoid air pollution and to simplify leaching processes. The leaching behavior of Sn, Ag, and Cu and the subsequent recovery of each metal component were examined during hydrochloric acid leaching and subsequent cementation process. The effects of the parameters such as hydrochloric acid concentration, leaching temperature, and agitation speed, on the dissolution of Sn, Ag and Cu are discussed.

### **EXPERIMENTS** 

### **Materials** 

The waste Pb-free solder of Sn-Ag-Cu series was obtained from a recycling company in Korea, which was generated from the fabricating processes of printed circuit boards for electronic home appliances. The solder contained 87.7 % Sn, 3.09 % Ag, and 0.85 % Cu as main components. The X-ray pattern (see Fig. 2) of the solder shows the presence of phases such as Sn and Ag3Sn. ### **Leaching procedures** 

The leaching tests of the wast

e Pb-free solder in stannic chloride solution were performed in a 500 dm<sup>3</sup> three-necked Pyrex glass reactor using a heating mantle to maintain temperature. The reactor was fitted with an agitator and a reflux condenser. The reflux condenser was inserted in one port to avoid solution loss at high temperatures. In a typical run, 200 dm<sup>3</sup> of acid solution (0.5−3 kmol m<sup>-3</sup> HCl) was poured into the reactor and allowed to reach the thermal equilibrium (30−90 °C). A 2g of the solder powder under 125 µm size was added, and the agitator was set at 200−600 rpm. During the experiment, 3 cm<sup>3</sup> of the solution was sampled periodically at a desired time interval. The sample was filtered with 0.45 µm membrane filter and then the filtrate was diluted with 5 % HNO3 solution for Cu and Ag analyses and 15% HCl solution for Sn analysis, respectively. At the end of the leaching tests, the entire volume remaining in the reactor was filtered when precipitate was observed, and then dried overnight at 105 °C for XRD. 

### **Analytical methods** 

The sample solutions were analyzed by an atomic absorption spectrometry (AA7000, Shimadzu Co. Ltd.) and an inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometry (ICPAES, JY-38 plus, Jobin Yvon Ltd.). The precipitates were also characterized by X-Ray Diffraction (Smartlab, Rigaku Co.). 

### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSION** 

The leaching tests of the waste Pb-free solder in hydrochloric acid solution with stannic chloride was carried out at agitation speeds in the range 200−600 rpm, and the effect of liquid film boundary diffusion surrounding the solid particles was investigated on the leaching efficiency of the solder in 1 kmol m<sup>-3</sup> HCl at 50 °C with 0.2 kmol m<sup>-3</sup> SnCl4. As seen in Fig. 3, the leaching efficiency of Sn are independent of the agitation speeds after 30 minutes. Therefore, in all subsequent leaching tests, a working agitation speed of 400 rpm was selected to ensure effective particle suspension in the solution while minimizing the effect of liquid film boundary diffusion surrounding the solid particles.

The waste Pb-free solder consists of tin, silver and copper. In the leaching tests in Figures 3-5, silver was not detected and copper concentration was determined to be extremely low concentration. ### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The hydrochloric acid leaching with stannic chloride was investigated to develop the recycling process of waste Pb-free solder. The leaching efficiency increased with increasing hydrochloric acid concentration and temperature. However, stannic ion precipitates in the reactor at more than 70 °C. Silver was not detected and copper concentration was extremely low in the leaching tests. Therefore, the results suggest that tin could be selectively leached using hydrochloric solution with stannic chloride.

### **ABSTRACT** 

Thermal techniques such as direct combustion, pyrolysis, gasification and cocombustion with plastic waste are some of the most effective methods for the treatment and recycling of Waste Electric and Electronic Equipment (WEEE). Currently, this type of waste is mainly treated thermally in incinerators (e.g. rotary kilns) to decompose plastics, to concentrate metals in the bottom and fly ashes. The concentrated metals (e.g. copper) can be supplied as secondary raw materials to metal smelters while the pyrolysis of plastics allows for the recovery of energy as fuel gas. However, WEEE such as printed circuit boards (PCBs) usually contain brominated flame retardants (BFRs). Hydrobromic acid (HBr) is known to be a product of the thermal decomposition of these materials. 

We thus studied the bromination of antimony oxide (Sb2O3), copper (Cu) and silver (Ag) by HBr that originates from BFRs such as Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) and Tetrabromobisphenol A - Tetrabromobisophenol A diglycidyl ether copolymer (TTDE). Additionally, we studied the possible volatilization of the formed bromides under an inert atmosphere over a wide temperature range. Thermo-gravimetric analysis (TGA) and a laboratory-scale furnace were used in this study. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Various treatment options based on conventional mechanical, physical, pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical processes are used for the recovery of metals from WEEE [1].  Pyrometallurgy is a traditional technology for the recovery of nonferrous metals as well as precious metals from WEEE. A typical pyrometallurgical process involves the pre-treatment of WEEE and the thermal treatment of scrap in incinerators to decompose plastics and to concentrate metals in the bottom ash. Concentrated metals such as copper and precious metals can be supplied as secondary raw materials to copper smelters to recover copper and precious metals [2]. 

Typicallly, the plastic components of electronic scrap are composed of polyethylene, polypropylene and polycarbonates enriched in brominated flame retardants (BFRs). TBBPA is the most widely produced BFR and is used in more than 70 % of the world’s electronic and electrical appliances [3]. The BFR present in waste plastic decomposes during thermal processing and this generates large amounts of gaseous HBr [4-9]. This gas can react with metals and their oxides in the waste

to form volatile bromides [10-12]. However, the mechanisms and extent of bromination as well as the distribution of the formed bromides have never been reported for metals such as copper and silver. 

Antimony oxide (Sb2O3), is often used with organobromine compounds such as TBBPA to produce a synergistic flame retardant effect. This particular effect and the bromination mechanism of the oxide have been investigated in several previous studies [13-18].  However, the bromination and volatility of Sb2O3 in association with TBBPA decomposition has not been thoroughly investigated. 

Therefore, the behavior of the oxide (Sb2O3) and metals (Cu, Ag) of interest during thermal treatment with typical BFRs are the subject of this study. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was used to evaluate the decomposition of selected BFRs such as TBBPA and TTDE. A laboratory-scale furnace was used to evaluate the behavior of Sb2O3, Cu and Ag during thermal decomposition of BFR and the volatilization of the formed bromides. 

### **EXPERIMENTAL METHODS** 

Thermo-gravimetric analysis (TGA) of the BFRs (TBBPA, TTDE) were carried out using a Rigaku Thermo Plus TG 8120. A sample of about 10 mg was placed in an open alumina (Al2O3) pan and heated from 100 to 1300 °C at a constant heating rate of 10 °C/min under an inert atmosphere. 

In the furnace experiment, mixtures of TBBPA+Sb2O3 (2.82:1 w/w), TTDE+Cu

About 1.5 g. of the sample (three pellets) was placed on a combustion boat located inside a quartz tube reactor and heated using a small furnace. A quartz wool filter was placed inside the reaction tube at the position where the temperature of the outgoing gases dropped to about 100<sup>o</sup> C to collect the condensable phase that vaporized from the sample. The temperature of the furnace was initially stabilized at 140<sup>o</sup> C for 40 minutes, and then increased to the desired temperature (in separate runs) at a heating rate of 10 oC/min under Argon gas flow of 50 mL/min. When the desired temperature was reached the reaction tube was cooled rapidly by blowing air onto the outside of the reaction tube to prevent secondary reactions. The inside of reaction tube was flushed with Argon gas for 1 h before each experiment and during cooling. 

The solid residue and the vaporized (condensed) phases were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD-Rigaku, Rint 220) and an electron probe microanalyzer (EPMAJeol, JXA-8200 WD/ED). The total amount of formed CuBr was 48% of the total amount of Cu, and only 0.4% was vaporized. The weight of the solid sample decreased by 68% at 1000<sup>o</sup> C. At this temperature, about 38% of the initial amount of copper vaporized in the form of CuBr. 

The fate of silver during thermal treatment in the presence of BFR in the small tube furnace was investigated using a mixture of TTDE+Ag (10:1 w/w), as shown in Fig. 3(b). At 600<sup>o</sup> C, the weight of the solid residue decreased by 67%. This was mainly associated with the decomposition and vaporization of the organic compounds. TIC chromatograms of the vaporized (condensed) phase were very similar to those obtained during the thermal treatment of TDDE+Cu within the same temperature range. At least 50% of the silver reacted with the HBr that evolved during the decomposition of TTDE and all the formed silver bromide (AgBr) remained in the residue. XRD revealed the abundant presence of silver bromide in the solid residue. At 1000<sup>o</sup> C, a further decrease in the total sample weight (75%) was noted. This was associated with the further degradation and vaporization of organic compounds, as well as an increase in the vaporization of AgBr. From analytical results, it was found that 47% of the initial amount of silver converted into AgBr of which 35% was found in the vaporized (condensed) phase and 12% remained in the residue. An XRD of the solid residue that was collected at this temperature (data not shown here) indicated the presence of metallic Ag as well as the remains of AgBr.

### **TAKING ADVANTAGE OF USED OILS FOR MANUFACTURING** **_IN SITU_ BLASTING AGENTS – THE CHILEAN EXPERIENCE.** 

Eduardo O. Berger _Head of Mining & Metallurgy Department Universidad Andrйs Bello – Viсa del Mar. eduardo.berger@unab.cl_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

In order to face more demanding environmental regulations imposed on mining activities in Chile, a significant number of open pit mines have decided to take advantage of recycled used oil generated by different types of mining equipment and use this material in the manufacturing of _in situ_ blasting agents, in a similar way as some other mining operations in USA and Canada do. Those blasting agents manufactured with some percentage of recycled used oil (usually 50%), allow achieving the same results in rock fragmentation and heave as compared to regular blasting agents manufactured using fuel oil only. Some mining companies in Chile which have already implemented this practice are

Escondida, Spence, Cerro Colorado (BHP); Los Bronces, El Soldado, Mantos Blancos (Angloamerican); Radomiro Tomic, Gaby (Codelco); Los Pelambres, El Tesoro (Antofagasta Minerals); Candelaria, El Abra (Freeport Mac Moran). The main steps to carry out a project like this are: a) Sampling of collected used oil at maintenance workshop; b) Physical and chemical analysis of representative samples of used oils, c) A set of lab and field trials; d) Analysis of the scheme used in the maintenance workshop for collecting and store used oil; e) Analysis to define the expected used oil consumption in accordance to the corresponding blasting agents consumption for the complete life of mine; f) Definition of a basic plant design and project feasibility; g) Government permit or authorization procedures. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The possibility to taking full advantage of used oils in the manufacture of blasting agents is presented as an interesting alternative for waste minimization and _in situ_ recovery with the additional benefit of reducing costs by replacing a percentage of fuel oil which, finally, translates into savings in raw materials. 

Waste or used oils, mainly from machinery used in mining operations themselves, are pre-treated to ensure operations are as smooth as if only diesel was being used. Originally, oil compositions correspond to complex mixtures of various types, such as lubricating, transmission, hydraulic oils, etc. Their initial composition is primarily hydrocarbons, nitrogen compounds containing oxygen, sulfur, trace metals, and a widerange of physical-chemical substances. While oil is being used, all these components and additives are physically and chemically affected, mainly as a result of sustained combustion within the vehicle engine or by the friction of moving parts. It is for this reason that oils adopt a dark color the can turn into a very intense black, mainly due to the presence of very fine carbon in suspension. Experiences using used oils to manufacture ANFO blasting agents from the park-based mining equipment conducted in other countries, mainly in large-size open pit mining operations, not only in Chile, but also in the U.S. and Canada have been successful. This has led mining operations such as BHP-Billiton Cerro Colorado and Escondida; Angloamerican Los Bronces and El Soldado; and Codelco Norte Radomiro Tomic to implement this great idea that contributes positively to the environment.

- Pumps for used oil, blends with fuel oil, and drain well 

- Filters for used oils, fuel oil, and blen

ds

- Civil works (slab parking, spill containment pit); pipes, valves and "fittings" control panel, illumination poles, etc.

### **Requirements and Parameters for Recycled Used Oils** 

Collection and / or Storage of Used Oils at Maintenance Workshop. 

It is the responsibility of each mining company interested in implementing this type of facility to put in place the following measures applicable to used oil collection: 

- Before being sent to collection tanks, used oils collected from mining equipment sitting in the maintenance workshop should be filtered in basket mesh filters, in order to eliminate at this stage large foreign particles (those of 150 microns or more). This will avoid, in particular, the presence of grit and metal particles. 

- Keep collection tanks and/or used oil storage points free from degreasers or other surfactants such as defoaming or cleaning detergents used in the engine. 

- Prevent these from mixing with used oils, paraffin and/or gasoil to ensure the future sensitivity or safety of explosives.

Permanent verification of the quality standards applicable to used oils for optimal performance of plant facility operation, explosive delivery trucks, and eventually blasted rocks at the mine will be of utmost importance. 

### **Parameters and Standards for Manufacturing Blasting Agents Incorporating Used Oils** 

The following are the parameters considered as standards for manufacturing blasting agents incorporating used oils:

### **Compatibility and Performance Tests for Blasting Agents Incorporating Used Oils** 

Compatibility testing as function of time is carried out both with respect to ammonium nitrate (prill) and with respect to a matrix or emulsion; where practicable and appropriate, the reactivity with aluminum can also be studied. Furthermore, the performance of blasting agents is established via the so-called ballistic tests which ultimately correspond to measurements of unconfined detonation velocity and sensitivity to initiation. 

Moreover, as established by IME (Institute of Makers of Explosives, USA), in its article "Safety Guidelines for Companies Authorized by the Mine Safety and Health Administration to Utilize Used

Vehicle Engine Oil in ANFO", the mixing proportion of used oils/fuel oil, should be in the ratio of 50/50. In this regard, main explosive providers in Chile (Enaex and Orica)have decided to adopt this recommendation as the basis or starting point on whose basis to establish the design and size in their facilities. Thus, the possibility of considering higher percentages of used oils in a blend with fuel oil contents as high as 75%, should be carefully studied, in particular, if the mine is located in a geographical location where ambient temperatures can get quite low.

The latter ratio is related to the increase of the viscosity sensitivity in used oil as temperature decreases, which causes side injection of the blend (used oil/fuel oil) to be more difficult to perform in the blasting-agent delivery trucks; and secondly, absorption times exhibited by the used oils/fuel oil blend to be the same. It should be noted also that the detonation velocity can have lower records especially with decreasing diameter hole. 

Therefore, and according to the above, it is emphasized that the decision to eventually increase the proportion of used oils in the blend should be made on a case-bycase basis. This decision should, of course, consider step-by-step and partial increases of used oil while taking good care of variations that might occur in detonation speed and rock fragmentation. 

Finally, it should be noted also that, despite the so-called "oxygen balance", Anfo prepared with a 50/50 proportion of used oil/fuel oil is very similar to Anfo manufactured only with diesel oil. However, used oils are not allowed for use in underground mines basically because of the lack of in-advance certainty as to whether the blend of used oils as compared to regular fuel oil is equally safe, from a chemical point of view; and, secondly, small-diameter blastholes commonly used in underground mines affect the efficiency of explosive chemical reactions during their detonation process increasing the probability of releasing noxious fumes. 

Finally, it is also necessary to note that, despite the so-called "oxygen balance" of Anfo when made with a proportion of Used Oil / Fuel Oil 50/50, is very similar to that made using oil as fuel only, however, to use underground mines is not allowed. As far as the above is concerned, main reasons to exclude used oils in underground mines are mainly, the difficulty to be sure in advance that blend of used oils as compared to regular fuel oil is nearly chemically talking and, secondly, small blasthole diameter commonly used in underground mines affect the efficiency of explosive chemical reactions during its detonation process increasing the probability to generate noxious fumes.

### **FUTURE DIRECTIONS FOR SCRAP MELTING IN COPPER SHAFT FURNACES** 

John R. Hugens _Fives North American Combustion, Inc. 885 River Cliff Court, Suwanee, Georgia, U.S.A.30024 John.Hugens@Fivesgroup.com_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Although the copper melting shaft furnace was developed primarily for the melting of copper cathodes, its use for the melting of copper scrap started immediately due to the need to recycle scrap copper tube and billet ends in tube mills. The scrap melting techniques developed in the tube mills eventually spread to wire and rod making plants as well. Today the favorable economics of melting scrap have induced many users to maximize the introduction of copper scrap in their shaft furnaces. The use of different grades of copper scrap affects the design, operation and quality of production of the furnaces in many different ways. Many different techniques have been utilized to accommodate the use of these materials. Future furnaces will utilize these techniques and develop new designs and procedures for handling them. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

310 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The use of scrap in the modern shaft furnace is actually an attempt to develop alternate feeds and operating methods for a furnace that was originally designed for another purpose. It is a customization and modernization of a process that was developed and piloted by Asarco for electro-refined cathodes to feed semi continuous and continuous casting processes. Most any plant that is converted to melt scrap for continuous casting will still need access to a high efficiency cathode melting furnace on demand due to fluctuations in material prices. This is most conveniently done in the same furnace. So, the simplified issue is really how much copper scrap, of what types, will a cathode melting furnace successfully use? 

The contemplated use of a vertical furnace for melting copper scrap significantly pre-dates the use of a shaft furnace for melting copper cathodes as shown in Figure-1 below [1].<sup>1</sup> 







Figure-1- Brassert Furnace [1] 

Since cathode melting shaft furnace are desiring to substitute various grades of copper scrap for cathodes, the potential abilities of cathode melting shaft furnaces shaft furnace for the melting of copper scrap have long been a matter of interest to the copper industry among tube, w

ire making and other manufacturing processes downstream of continuous and semi-continuous casting plants. This is due to the appearance of relative economies of using copper scrap as feed and also the need to process scrap and to recycle out-of-specification and used material returned by customers in the same furnaces. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

311 

The well-known copper melting shaft furnace, as invented and designed by Asarco Central Research Department in the 1960s was developed for the use of melting copper cathodes. However charges of up 100% anode copper scrap were soon used at some locations. Mixed charges of blister copper and secondary copper were contemplated [2]<sup>2</sup> , but the use of these furnaces was not widespread, and they faced many operational difficulties, and in many cases have ceased to operate. 









Figure 2-Asarco Shaft Furnace [3] 

Soon after the development of the Asarco furnace, the inventors communicated to their licensees the policy that the furnace was to be used for cathodes only with very limited amounts of scrap. Nevertheless it was not long before questions started to arise about how much scrap the furnace could melt. And Asarco itself was experimenting with how much tube scrap it could melt in this type of furnace design. The original diameter of the furnace was designed for the copper cathodes of the 1960’s era (137 cm. to 182 cm I.D. for the furnace), the refractories were optimized for this use (oxide bonded silicon carbide) but trials were run with different types and grades of scrap to see how much scrap could be utilized. 

At one time, in failed melting test, Asarco attempted the charging a furnace with scrap radiators to see the result. Copious notes were taken, including the different colors 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

312 

of flames emerging from the tap hole. The conclusion at the time reiterated that the furnace was better suited for melting cathodes. 

The official answer to the scrap melting question for many years was that a furnace could receive 30% of a mixture of loose and baled No. 1 scrap mixed with cathodes. This amount has been exceeded in many places but it still may be regarded as a baseline for a cathode melting furnace that has not otherwise been enhanced for the feeding of scrap materials. This quantity also matched the scrap return rate in many tube mills. This rule of operation still left the open question of how much scrap of various types a furnace could possibly run with improved operating procedures and modifications. One of the main problems emerging from practice was not melting itself but the problem of slag removal from the launders which became too for the operators onerous at levels about this. 

“Heretofore there have been many attempts to melt impure copper in a vertical furnace which was fired with a liquid or gaseous fuel. These prior attempts, however, failed because of the difficulty to discharge the slags resulti

ng either from the impurities in the blister copper and in the impure copper, or from the reaction products of these impurities with the refractory lining of the furnace, Hence, it has never been possible to melt in a economical way blister copper and impure copper scrap in a vertical furnace which is fired with a liquid fuel or a gaseous fuel[4].”<sup>4</sup> 

However, it was well known that the melting of certain amounts of scrap was a practice used at almost every tube mill with a shaft furnace. It soon became clear that under the right conditions much more scrap could be fed into a furnace successfully up to 100% of the charge, especially if the furnace was already hot and running for a few days in advance of the charging. 

The most successful general adaptation of the furnace to scrap melting to date has been charging a furnace with tank house anode scrap. Melting 100% content anode scrap proved successful as some intrepid users in the late 1960's pioneered the use of the furnace for melting scrap anodes. In this configuration the furnace seemed to be capable of continuous operation for weeks on end.  Even though the oxygen level of the scrap was high at about 1300 ppm, the amount of slag produced during melting appeared manageable at the furnace tap-hole. Many of the Anode scrap furnaces also charged limited amounts of lower sulfur blister copper up to the point that it could be tolerated in the associated tank-house. The consistency of the feed and lower surface area of the anode scrap relative to other scrap streams appears the make the operation of the shaft furnace on anode scrap industrially feasible. About 7 of these furnaces have been built or converted in size ranges from 20 to 60 tons per hour. 

In sum, the melting of anode scrap has been successfully practiced at several smelters, and has been documented as well as the melting of high levels of DHP return scrap. But the melting of high levels of purchased scrap containing wire, especially scap of the No. 2 designation has remained a problem and has not been documented in detail. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

313 

The amount of slag production from these more finely divided materials appears to be greater. 

### **ATTRACTIVE ADVANTAGES** 

The relative efficiency of the shaft furnace for melting scrap compared to reververatory melting was never in question. In fact the efficiency of the furnace increased up to a certain point when using increased quantities of scrap of different sorts. (This is a relationship that needs to be explored more deeply). Most operators sense a relationship between the porosity of the furnace charge (ratio of solids to voids) in the furnace to the tap-hole area and the efficiency of the furnace. If this relationship could be better defined, optimum energy efficiencies with respect to charge practice could be established. 

Charging the furnace with small pieces reduces the gas flow through the furnace column and increases the surface

area for heat exchange, but the number of small pieces can increase to the point where flow decreases and energy transfer appears to be inhibited due to low flow. As a consequence a mixed charge with cathodes or large pieces is common practice to provide channels to promote heat exchange to the smaller pieces of copper in the furnace. Surface area and gas flow are inversely related in the furnace but both factors enhance heat exchange. 

The largest advantage to scrap charging is economic. The premium available for melting no 1 (99%) scrap can vary from 0 to $.25 per lb. with respect to the LME cathode price with a typical recent value of $.05 per lb. raising the potential benefit of melting scrap over cathodes from zero to $50,000,000 dollars per year with a 100,000.00 ton per year operation. 

Fuel consumption can be as low as 950 MJ. Btu per ton of scrap melted, compared to 1,266 MJ  per ton of scrap melted as a relative number for cathodes. 

### **DISADVANTAGES** 

The primary disadvantage to melting scrap copper in the shaft furnace is the presence of impurities not normally found in cathode copper. Unless the scrap is very pure ETP wire, it is likely to have been contaminated with other metals including aluminum and lead, or with burnt copper wire, all of which cause problems in physical melting and in the chemistry of the end product. 

The majority of scrap melting furnaces do not provide feed for processes which provide copper for the highest quality products such as for thin walled tube or ultra-fine wire, or magnet wire production. However, it is clear that for many other segments of the market, such as water tube or building wire the end product can be highly suitable for

use.  So, the economics are favorable even though the tasks of operating the furnace become more difficult for the operators 

The slag and copper oxides that the melting copper scrap sloughed offcan fill the hearth of the furnace and shut it down within hours of starting a high scrap charge. This creates severe operating problems and maintenance problems including the destruction of burners and furnace and launder linings. 

As a consequence refractory costs related to scrap melting can be as high as $400,000 per year including installation. But with the higher potential returns from scrap melting this is only a small fraction of the cost. In almost all cases the refractory lining life of the furnace is compromised by scrap melting. 

Scrap also introduces the potential for the unpredictability of impurities in the end product, as one bucket or bail of scrap can differ markedly from the next. So, some method of averaging the charge chemistry is desirable 

Different impurities present in the copper scrap can produce changes in the behavior of the furnace launders and down-stream equipment. The most notable is usually aluminum which produces a thermally reflective slag surface on the copper. During aluminum excu

rsions the temperatures of the launders and the holding furnace can rise to a white heat and most often the furnace equipment must be drained and cleaned to cure the problem. 

Extended down time and equipment costs are the outcome of both of these problems. 

Operators of cathode melting shaft furnaces have enjoyed the ability to run without bag filters because of the low opacity and low VOC and particulate concentration of the furnace off gas. These advantages disappear when melting most varieties of scrap. Even the cleanest scrap charge, by appearance, will contain drawing oils and finishing compounds that will create smoke and fume on melting. 

Various technologies such as bag filters, venture scrubbers, candle filters, afterburners and regenerative thermal oxidizers are a necessity to meet local environmental requirements.

### **Modifications to the furnace hearth and walls** 









Figure 3-Vogel Hearth Modifications [5] 

Plants that melt scrap have developed proprietary designs for continuously cleaning the hearths and burners of the furnace in order to run continuously with high scrap charges up to 100 percent for extended periods. An example of one solution to this is US patent 5,890,889 by Barstow<sup>6</sup> which describes refractory stand-offs in front of the burners to prevent solidification of copper and slag by holding them away from the burners[6]. Similar hearth modifications were proposed by Vogel in his 1974 patent [7].<sup>7</sup> 

There are many other solutions to this issue of re-freezing of slag and copper relating to burner positioning, tap-hole size and other features such as covering the hearth with multiple domes to improve gas circulation[8].<sup>8</sup> While the number of solutions is many, this points out one of the most difficult aspects of melting scrap, maintaining fluidity of the melt. Clarkson in U.S. patent 4,059,102 describes methods of using oxygen combustion to increase the fluidity of the melt by superheating it and methods of shaping the hearth to maintain high temperatures and prevent solidification. 

Cathode melting furnaces need to be re-designed to allow sufficient access for lances and other equipment into the hearth area. However adding too much access area in

The largest practical tap holes are in the size range of 250 x 250 mm. Many users have found that extending the height of the tap hole is more effective than increasing the width. 

### **Modified Operating Practices** 

While the melting of cathodes requires little intervention by the operator into the functioning of the furnace, scrap melting requires almost constant vigilance by the operator, especially in the areas of the tap-hole and lower burners. Since scrap produces a relatively large amount of slag that can plug the furnace tap-hole, the operator must become very aware of both the sound of the furnace and the potential visible and instrumented clues which indicate the occlusion of burners and the tap-hole. In the worst cases burners require almost constant cleaning and maintenance. 

Over the years different melting shops developed different practices and recipes for melting scrap including melting purchased scrap steams with certain quantities of blister copper and other materials. The formulas and methods of different operators are dependent on both the scrap materials that they receive and the operating schedules of the various plants. Generally the choice is made to mix the different streams as homogenously as possible, with the exception of only charging fine materials, such as saw chips, periodically, as these materials often fall to the furnace hearth, temporarily cooling it. 

Independently some users began experimenting with the practice of charging large amounts of scrap in copper rod operations to produce HCFR grade copper. This practice was successful and perfected in some plants. 

Because of their operating schedules, some plants tend to schedule down times when slag can be manually removed from the furnace and burners. It is not unusual to hear of three or five day campaigns for melting large amounts of scrap. 

Other plants tend to blend the copper scrap with some degree of cathodes in order to wash the accumulated slag out of the furnace. 

Slags and their operating characteristics are identified rapidly by successful operators who develop means for dealing with them and, if possible, clearing them from the furnace tap-hole. Often the only mean of clearing the tap-hole is with lances or oxyfueled burner devices. Less severe blockages can be removed with expendable wooden poles or steel lances and spoons which must be coated with bone-ash before use and frequently hammered clean of slag accretions. 

### **Refractories in use for melting of copper scrap** 

There is no single refractory solution for the effects of the impurities on copper scrap on copper melting furnaces.  The refractory practice in these furnaces requires

Refractories need to be chosen with respect to properties the chemical impurities in the copper and the degree of oxidation required for the metal. For example Nickel impurities have a rapid and immediate effect silicon carbide materials. Because of this furnaces exposed to nickel in anything greater than low ppm levels or high concentrations of iron are usually lined with some form of basic brick rather than the traditional silicon carbide lining. With refractories, minimizing the yearly cost, including labor and materials, should be the goal, respective of the down time required for replacement. The savings on inexpensive refractories should subtract the cost of differential down time required for their more rapid replacement. 

Once the furnace lining is selected based on the expected charge material impuriteis, the configuration of the furnace burners and the tap-hole design need to be considered. As a general rule the higher the percentage of loose scrap in the charge, the more firepower has to be concentrated in the lower part of the furnace. Scrap that falls from the top of the furnace to the bottom in solid form removes substantial head from the furnace hearth as it melts. Drops of copper falling from above the hearth are then potentially deprived of superheat. When the ratio of solid copper arriving at the hearth vs. liquid is higher than a certain percentage a plaque of copper forms and shields the hearth from radiated heat. At this point the furnace can no longer be operated as a melting furnace and operations need to be discontinued until the cold copper is removed from the hearth.

### **Nitride Bonded Silicon Carbide** 

Nitride bonded silicon carbide consists of silicon carbide bonded with silicon nitride _,_ formed during a nitriding process. Silicon nitride bonded SiC is not wetted by copper metal whereas regular silicate bonded SiC is wetted, allowing metal penetration into the pores structure which can cause subsequent thermal spalling. Silicon nitride bonded bricks also have an improved resistance against copper oxide attack due to their density, and their significant higher mechanical strength, which gives superior impact and abrasion resistance -make them an excellent choice for impact area shapes [10].<sup>10</sup> Nitride bodned silicon carbide is traditionally produced in a semi-continuous tunnel kiln process. Because the nitrogen must diffuse through the heated shapes, sizes of traditional nitride-bonded shapes may be limited to approximately 100 mm.in thickness.

### **Oxide Bonded Silicon Carbide** 

Oxide bonded silicon carbide is designed for exceptional wear and corrosion resistance.  It can be formed into very intricate and precise shapes [10].<sup>11</sup> The silicon carbide is heated with a binding material in a neutral combustion environment. 

It is traditionally produced in a large domed kiln which is heated for several weeks. 

This composition, in the form of mix-carbofrax A978 was traditionally used for the Asarco designed shaft furnaces. It served many furnaces for many years obtaining furnace lives of many years and hundreds of thousands of tons. It use has largely been replaced in the USA by Nitride bonded products. In Europe and the Far East, it is still the dominant compound used in shaft furnace linings. 

Some would argue that the method of producing Oxide bonded silicon carbide is not possible in tunnel kilns which produce the majority of the product. 

### **Chrome Alumina Refractories** 

The chrome-alumina refractories, composed of alumina mixed with varying amounts of chrome oxide have shown promise in areas o

f the furnace subjected to intense oxidation. They exhibit a high resistance to thermal shock and cycling similar to silicon carbide, and resist penetration by copper. However, they are not as resistant to mechanical wear. They have been used in burner blocks and in oxidizing areas of the furnace hearth in anode melting furnaces. Their high cost, however, restricts their use to problem areas in the furnace subject to oxidizing conditions.

But, in those cases where chemical oxidation attack is especially severe, they may out-perform the silicon carbide refractories on a cost per ton melted basis.

### **Combustion system configuration design and settings** 

Original specifications for the ratio control settings of the furnaces are often ignored in copper scrap melting and a wide variety of operator opinions are used to establish burner settings, based largely upon individual opinions about the furnace operation under various conditions. 

In general the combustion conditions used in copper no. 1 scrap melting are more reducing than those used for melting cathodes. It is assumed that this is to inhibit slag formation inside the furnace. Settings are generally 1-2 percent richer in terms of excess fuel than those used in cathode melting. However operation with too much excess fuel can lead to plugging the burners with copper that has cooled small pieces which fall in front of the burner. 

Several operations have found it advantageous to apply tangentially fired burners in the upper section of the furnace to assist in melting finely divided scrap. The application of these burners appears to inhibit the fall of cold copper material to the hearth of the furnace, thus increasing hearth temperature and reducing the tendency of the tap-hole to block [12].<sup>12</sup> 

### **Charging** 

Judicious mixing of different types of scrap can minimize production of slag. As a general rule, the mixing of ETP scrap with DHP scrap produces a large amount of phosphorus oxide slag. This extra slag production can be avoided with diligence by separating the scrap types. 

Charge buckets and devices for charging the furnace designed for cathode charging are seldom the right size and capacity for receiving copper sc

rap. So a furnace designed to melt scrap and cathodes must have a design of the charging system that will accept both types of materials.

### **FUTURE DIRECTIONS** 

Shaft furnaces customized by vendors for scrap melting are beginning to appear. Publications implying the shaft melting of copper scrap and its various forms and strategies are widely available from vendors. Detailed descriptions of the processes and procedures are generally not available and are closely guarded information. 

Melting operations may or may not have a refining operation attached downstream of it. Such a refining operation may have one or two furnaces in the case of two furnaces they may operate in sequential batch fashion. In the case of a single holding/refining furnace, the furnace is usually used as a final polishing and homogenizing step. The primary function of these refining steps is to remove iron in the slag phase through oxidation and reduction of the melt. Some operations have used electromagnetic stirring in the bath to promote the refining of the metal. 

The design of copper melting shaft furnaces tends to be based on copying previous designs with the input of operator intuition. Trial and error is a large factor. Significant leverage on the problems that these furnaces have could be gained by adopting scientific principles instead of relying solely on operator and designer opinion. 

The efficiency of the furnace increases when using scrap and then decreases as the amount of finely divided material increases past a certain point. This is a relationship which needs to be explored theoretically and correlated with other furnace design variables. Experimental analysis of the effects of packing of a shaft are perhaps the best route forward as little work on the flow of gas through the complex geometry of scrap shapes exist. 

Manual scrap sorting has sometimes been employed as a method of improving purchased scrap to ensure that the charge contains no unwanted impurities. This can be a very successful strategy if labor costs are sufficiently low. Hopefully mechanized methods of scrap sorting will become more widely used in the computer age. Some suppliers of mining rock sorting machines are optimistic that they can solve the problem of sorting scrap materials. 

It seems reasonable that 96-97% copper is the maximum that any normal configuration of the Asarco type furnace would be able to melt at this time. Beyond this limit, rotary furnaces, traditional reverberatory furnaces or shaft-reverberatory hybrids become more economical because slag can be removed from them more easily. But the ultimate goal in the design of this type of fur

nace will be a simple shaft design from which slag and metal can be tapped and separated without intractable problems with clearing the tap-hole. Ideally this furnace could return to melting only cathodes without great difficulty.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The process features of secondary copper smelting with pyroprocessing and the structure of NGL furnace together with its combustion, nitrogen mild agitation and gas cleaning systems are analyzed and introduced in this paper. Operation practices in several secondary copper smelters in China with complete NGL furnace process are summarized in terms of operation steps, major process parameters and technical-economic results. NGL furnace process with complete equipment is elaborated with significant advantages including high production efficiency, low energy consumption, efficient reductant utilization, no black smoke escape from the closed vessel, minimum hazardous gas emission, less CO2/NOx emission, good environment protection, and high level of operation safety and automation. The further development of NGL furnace process is also discussed in this paper. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

324 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Pyroprocessing technology for secondary copper smelting differs great

ly from that for molten blister copper smelting. In the past, most smelters in China adopted stationary reverberatory furnaces for copper scrap smelting and thus were always challenged with the facts of inefficient utilization of oxidant and reductant, low level of automation, high labor intensity, bad operation environment and heavy pollution. Some smelters have adopted titling furnaces with progress in environment protection, operation safety and automation, but titling furnaces still have weak points of poor heat and mass transfer due to no bath agitation and difficulties in operation and maintenance because of its complicated structure and incomplete gas cleaning system. NGL furnace<sup>[1]</sup> process with complete equipment has been developed by China Nerin Engineering Co., Ltd. especially to cope with those shortages of current secondary copper smelting technologies and equipment. Advantages of NGL furnaces have been proven by practical operations such as high production efficiency, low energy consumption, good environment protection and high level of operation safety and automation and now have been recommended as a priority selection in secondary copper smelters in China. 

### **FEATURES OF SECONDARY COPPER SMELTING WITH PYROPROCESSING** 

Sources of secondary copper are extensive and it is of complicated composition and various shapes and contains organic substances. Therefore, the development of pyroprocessing technology and equipment for secondary copper smelting has to have the following considerations: 

### **Time Consuming During Feeding and Melting** 

Secondary copper fed into furnaces is all solid cold materials in clumps, powders and packaged filament materials. It is time consuming to feed and melt secondary copper. During secondary copper smelting with pyroprocessing, the time for feeding and melting accounts for more than half of the operation cycle and the fuel consumption during feeding and melting accounts for more than 80% of the total consumption, so production efficiency and energy consumption of secondary copper smelting with pyroprocessing are greatly influenced by its feeding and melting rate. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

325 

### **Complicated Materials and Difficulty of Refining** 

The impurity content in secondary copper is normally around 4~20% while 0.5~2% in molten blister. Besides metal elements including Pb, Zn, As, Sb, Bi, Ni, Fe, etc., secondary copper usually contains halogen elements such as F, Cl, Br and organic substances. Several stages of oxidation and slag formation, sometimes even basic slag formation, are normally required in secondary copper smelting to remove different impurities. 

### **Large Volume of Slag and Frequent Slag Tapping** 

The slag yield from secondary copper smelting is normally 10~20% or even higher in case of low-grade feed materials. The slag contains 10~35% Cu and is large in volume and high in viscosity. Therefore the structure of secondary copper

refining furnace should be designed as convenient for slag tapping. 

### **High Volatile Content in Gas and Consequently High Demanding of Gas Cleaning System** 

A large quantity of volatiles will be in gas during secondary copper smelting, including Pb, Zn, and unburned organic substances and the dust content in gas sometimes can be more than 100 g/Nm<sup>3</sup> . Serious cementation might occur at the furnace exit, flue and waste heat recovery system without proper control in production and thus causes trouble for gas cleaning. If materials into furnaces are not properly pre-treated and still contain organic substances, toxic components might be created during refining. It shall be one of the major considerations for furnace and gas handling design to eliminate dioxin and other noxious gases. 

### **INTRODUCTION OF NGL FURNACE AND ITS SUPPORTING SYSTEMS** 

NGL furnace was named by taking N from Nerin, the short of China Nerin Engineering Co., Ltd., G from “Gu Ti Wu Liao” (which means solid materials in Chinese) and L from “Lu Zi” (which means furnace in Chinese). 

### **Structure of NGL Furnace** 

A NGL furnace is a cylinder type rotatable furnace. Its vessel is supported by carrying rollers and rotated 360 degrees by a driving system made up of a motor and a set of gear box unit. There is a big door for charging as well as for deslagging on one side of

the vessel and a quick-replaceable oxidation-reduction device on the other side, while the bottom is equipped with nitrogen mild agitation systems.
