### **Combustion System** 

Secondary copper melting rate influences greatly upon production efficiency and energy consumption and it is essential to select and install a proper combustion system. An evaluation and computer simulation study on secondary copper melting rate and heat balance value inside the vessel has been made with various fuels and combustion modes according to the structure and actual dimensions of NGL furnaces. It is determined after the study to adopt a combustion system with industrial oxygen and fuel mixed inside the furnace. The fuel can be gas fuels like natural gas or liquid fuels like heavy oil. The combustion system is characterized by wide and even distribution high temperature zone, 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

327 

as well as the ability to reduce waste gas emission greatly and fuel consumption efficiently. 

Computer simulation during furnace design and results are referred to for adjusting the vessel structure, bur

ner arrangement and parameters repeatedly to obtain an optimal heat distribution in NGL furnaces, which not only increases melting rate and saves fuels but also reduces gas volume by nearly 3/4. 

### **Nitrogen Mild Agitation System and Oxidation Reduction System** 

Secondary copper refining requires air blowing during oxidation and slag formation stage which normally takes long time when secondary copper contains high impurity content. Afterwards, it is required to add reductant to remove excess oxygen in liquid copper. In both reverberatory furnace and tilting furnace, oxidation or reduction is achieved by blowing air or reductant into the furnace simply with several nozzles. It is difficult to mix either air or reductant evenly with a large amount of liquid copper, which causes inefficient utilization of air or reductant. It is a bottleneck resulting in refining process low in efficiency and long in time. Inefficient reductant utilization also means a great quantity of unburned carbon will be into gas and cause pollution of black smoke. 

Multiple nitrogen mild agitation systems have been carefully arranged at the bottom of NGL furnace according to simulation results. Positions and angles of oxidation-reduction air nozzles on the vessel sides are adjusted, which forms a vertical gas distribution network of nitrogen mild agitation and oxidation-reduction systems to achieve excellent heat and mass transfer of liquid copper during the whole refining process and avoid any dead zone of melt. Therefore, both oxidation and reduction efficiencies are greatly increased. Moreover, another benefit of nitrogen mild agitation systems is to move slag for quick and easy deslagging. 

Nitrogen mild agitation systems are made of corundum in slit type structure with long life cycle. 

### **Gas Cleaning System** 

A stationary exhaust hood is installed over the end of NGL furnace. A special device is applied to make the vessel rotate easily and seal to the hood without gas or dust leakage. A fugitive gas hood is installed over the furnace door to collect fugitive gas from the furnace mouth during charging and deslagging. The fugitive gas hood is fixed on and rotates with the vessel. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

328 

The NGL furnace gas cleaning system adopts a process flow of secondary combustion, spray cooling, air cooling and bag filtration especially for treatment of large number of volatiles and unburned carbon and organic substances produced from the process. The spray cooling system can cool down the gas from 1000<sup>o</sup> C quickly to 300<sup>o</sup> C to avoid generation of dioxin. If secondary copper contains F, Br, S, etc., it is required to add desulphurization, carbon absorption and other equipment. 

Process parameters are strictly controlled in each step of gas cleaning to finally collect dry dusts, eliminate pollution of black smoke and minimize emission of harmful gases and CO2/NOx. 

### **Automation and Process Contro

l of NGL Furnace** 

In order to improve operation efficiency and achieve safe and easy operation of NGL furnaces, seven advanced control systems, which combine PLC and DCS control technologies, are installed and cover the whole production range from NGL furnace operation till interconnection of anode casting. 

- Drive control system includes accurate vessel rotation angle positioning and stopping. Each NGL furnace is equipped with a separate PLC control system which allows programming for different applications and communications of internal and external data. 

- Combustion control is to calculate the ratio of oxygen and fuel based on hearth temperature and to adjust flow rate and pressure of fuel and oxygen as well as burner ignition. 

- Nitrogen mild agitation control is to control nitrogen flow rate and pressure and to monitor temperature of nitrogen mild agitation device. 

- Oxidation and reduction control provides air and reductant flow rate and pressure control and automatic switch between air and reductant. 

- Gas cleaning control covers gas temperature and pressure detection in the process, automatic water spray cooling and pressure control inside the furnace.

- Interlock between drive of NGL furnace and operation of cast machine ensures operation accuracy and safety. 

- Utilities and auxiliaries control includes monitoring, regulation and interlock of cooling water system of NGL furnace and cast machine, oxygen and air compressor as well as power supply and distribution system. 

The above control systems are centralized in a control room of NGL furnace and all the monitoring and operation are made via the computer screen. 

High automation level makes NGL furnaces not only easy and efficient in operation but also safe in operation and low in emission. **OPERATION PRACTICES AND TECHNICAL-ECONOMIC RESULTS OF NGL FURNACE**

### **SCHENCK PROCESS DOME VALVE** 

The valves used in pneumatic injection systems have often been its downfall. Many pyrometallurgical process users report the valve as its number one failure issue. Many valves have a short life of hours or days. Schenck Process’s Pneumatic Conveying and Pneumatic Injection solutions all use a valve known as the Dome Valve.  This valve delivers unrivalled performance allowing Schenck Process Pneumatic Injection Systems to work on an annual planned maintenance basis with high availability. 

The Schenck Process Dome Valve was originally designed and patented by Clyde Process in 1974 and has been used in a wide variety of materials handling applications; the valve has become an industry standard. The valve configuration, shown in Figure 7 & 8, comprises of a dome shaped closure mounted on half shafts that is moved through 90 degrees by means of a pneumatic cylinder. A rubber seal mounted at the entry to the valve is inflated by compressed air when the valve is in the closed position in order to obtain a gas tight closure. When the valve is opened, the seal is first

deflated, causing it to retract away from the dome; the dome then moves to the open position. In this way there is no direct contact between the dome and seal while the dome is moving, hence the associated abrasive wear of the seal is avoided. 

A seal life of typically 500,000 operating cycles, equivalent to more than 2 years operation, is achieved. This valve is seen as the most reliable in the industry and is used by many operators in demanding environments as their chosen standard. The valve can be modified through cooling, seal types and finishes to suit a large range of materials. The resulting technology has resolved the valve problem for most applications used for pneumatic conveying and injection solutions. Valves are available with outlets from 50 to 650mm and versions are available up to 750C operating temperature.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The recovery of materials from urban waste has become progressively important with wastes providing a variety of resources, whose processing can lead to an environmentally sustainable solution to metal availability. Recycling of metals such as copper makes the recovery attractive from technical and economical points of view, as the copper content in several discarded products can be much higher than the corresponding concentration of copper from various ores. This article provides an overview on the recovery of copper from several waste streams and reports an experimental investigation on the recovery of copper from end–of–life electric and electronic equipment (e–waste). In–depth investigations have been carried out to recover copper from printed circuit boards. Experimental results have shown that a heat treatment at 1150°C over a period of time generated two types of solid residues: a metallic phase and a carbonaceous phase. Copper and copper alloys were recovered in the metallic residue achieving a high recovery after the heat treatment.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Waste management is becoming increasingly important in recent years. Increasing human activity has resulted in millions of tons of wastes being landfilled worldwide, that has a high impact not only on health, but also on the environment. However, wastes can be a big reservoir of different types of resources including materials and energy. Metals recovery from the urban waste has become very important especially for metals such as copper, aluminium and steel. Many countries have made moves to ensure effective recycling either through legislation or end-of–life product collections. The copper content in some of the used products can be much higher than the corresponding concentration of copper from various ores, which makes recycling and metal recovery attr

active from technical and economical points of view. Copper is among some of the most commonly used metals in a wide range of applications; its usage is third in the world after iron and aluminium. 

Both copper scrap and end–of–life copper alloys are found in a variety of solid wastes. According to the classification required by different organizations/countries [1], copper containing solid waste can be broadly classified into five broad categories: Construction and Demolition Waste (C&D), Waste of Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE or E–waste), End–of–Life Vehicles (ELV), Industrial Waste (IW) and Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) including Sewage Sludge in a dry basis (SS) and Hazardous Wastes (HW). Some of the key sources of copper scrap include wires and cables, tubes, piping and electronic scrap from C&D and WEEE. While the basic waste treatment is carried out in smelting/refining facilities with approaches quite similar to those used to process copper ores, the choice of recycling techniques used depends on the waste characteristics. The specific advantage of electric arc furnaces (EAF) as well as other smelters employed to melt copper materials is that both these processes can be used for different types of alloys and are not very specific to a given type of feed material. 

In this article, an in–depth review has been carried out to identify various resources of waste copper, their relative proportions, current technologies and the challenges to recover the metal in an environmentally safe and sustainable manner. In addition, we report on an experimental investigation on the recovery of copper from e– waste through heat treatment at high temperatures.

A variety of copper resources can be recovered from the construction and demolition waste. Copper metal is commonly used in building wiring, plumbing, pipes, tubes, air–conditioning, refrigeration, gas distribution and heating, among many others [2]. These end–of–life components are excellent resources of waste copper and alloys. In Asia, the building and construction sector is one of the largest sector of copper usage (~15%) and represents an important scrap source [3]. The copper content in C&D can

Copper wires and cables can be divided into three categories: above–ground, which is high–grade scrap and therefore easily recycled; on– the–ground, that has several types of impurities, is usually mixed with other wastes and also may have different coverings and sizes; and below–ground/underwater, that requires complex processing and generally contains impurities such as lead coatings and grease [5]. 

Pyrometallurgical processes are commonly employed to recycle C&D copper scraps. The steps include size reduction, smelting, converting, fire refining and electro refining processes, where the copper wa

stes can be fed, determined by the grade of the metal [5]. Smelting process for low–grade scrap is generally carried out in Blast Furnaces, Top–Blown Rotary Converters and Electric Furnaces, which can treat miscellaneous copper materials. The melted product is black copper, which contains ~75–80% copper [6], which is then transferred to the converting process. The product is rough copper, typically containing 95% Cu [5,7], which is then, fire refined and cast into anodes of 98.5% purity. Electro–refining is the last step, which requires longer time to treat it as scraps may contain significant levels of impurities; nickel, tin and platinum– group residues are removed from copper [8]. Most significant impurities in this type of residue are lead and tin, which come from bronze, solder and slag and zinc from scrap brass. 

Recycling of underground cables has several technical challenges, mainly due to their flammability, covering, aluminium and lead present in the material. Most of the C&D is still being landfilled. In US, about  35% to 45% the residues are disposed in special C&D landfills, while about 20% to 40% is disposed in MSW landfills [9]. Environmental problems have been reported when C&D residues are mixed with residential wastes, such as the production of gaseous hydrogen sulphide. Also, when the C&D has a higher moisture content – around 14% to 16% – it can be degraded and lixiviate the soil and contaminate groundwater [9]. 

### **Electrical and Electronic Equipment Waste** 

End–of–life electric and electronic equipment can be divided into ten categories, such as large and small household appliances, consumer and IT & communications equipment, among others [10,11]. The relative copper content of a range of electronic wastes varies depending on the device, e.g. printed circuit boards have between 10% and 20% of copper [12,13]. Pyrometallurgical processes are the key approaches used to recover non–ferrous and precious metals from e–waste, including incineration, smelting, slag formation, melting and reactions in a gas phase at high temperatures [14,15]. Some well–known processes are Noranda, Rцnnskar and Umicore. In Noranda and Rцnnskar, the pyrometallurgical steps mentioned in C&D are carried out to treat e–wastes [16-18]. In the Umicore process several wastes are treated simultaneously [19], and various stages are required to recover different metals [12,13].

A number of studies have been carried out to recover copper from e–waste at high temperatures. Various techniques employed to recover copper include employment of slag forming material [20], mixture of e–waste with salts [21,22], as well as with waste copper slag [23], etc. Pyrolysis studies have also been carried out in a range of temperatures [24-26]. Recycling of copper and other metals from e–waste has several technical challenges that need to be faced, such as recovery of metals from the slag, production of dioxins due to

halogenated flame retardants present in e–wastes, the use of organics as an energy source and employment of other processes such as hydrometallurgical or electrochemical techniques to enhance metal recovery [11,12]. 

### **End–of–Life Vehicles** 

Several sources of copper are present in end–of–life vehicles, such as wires in electrical circuits, car and truck radiators, brake systems and induction motors in electric vehicles [27]. Copper and copper alloys are also used in trains, ships and airplanes. The transport sector accounts for nearly 15% of copper used in Asia [3], the copper content in ELV can amount up to 1.4% [1]. After dismantling, three copper streams can be obtained: the first corresponds to the radiator, which can be smelted and refined if a tin/lead solder was employed in its manufacturing; or directly smelted and recycled without refining if other type of solders or brazes were used, such as copper/brass radiators [5]. The second source is the non–ferrous metal scrap, where aluminium and zinc are found along with copper. This stream remains after car’s shredding and the magnetic removal of iron and steel. Main methods to separate copper are handpicking, air tabling and heavy–media separation. Mixtures of copper–aluminium–zinc can be smelted and copper may be recovered, as aluminium and zinc can be removed as slag. However, as these metals are part of the slag, these are generally lost and remain unrecovered [5]. 

The third source of the metal is the automotive shredding residue (ASR) that can contain up to 3% copper. This stream remains after the separation of iron and steel and non–ferrous metal scrap. Various materials and impurities present along with copper are basically dust, plastics and organic matter, fluff from seat cushions, and fragments of fabric and carpet. While this residue can be treated, it is generally landfilled [5]. The recycling of the shredded residue has been carried out to some extent by pyrometallurgical processes along with other waste streams. As the copper smelting process requires high amounts of energy, a treatment proposed by Jalkanen [28] involves the co–smelting of e–wastes with ASR to enhance the generation of heat as well as copper content. The impurities present in both wastes such as lead, tin or zinc do not require pre–treatment, and these can be removed as part of the slag [28]. The key environmental issues regarding ELVs are organic substances, such as polymers and cellulose fibre products. Also, composites and other non–metallic materials together with polymers tend to increase the proportion of ASR. Typical pollutants present in these materials are polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB) and hydrocarbons [29].

### **Industrial Waste** 

Industrial wastes may be divided into two groups: industrial electrical equipment waste (IEW) and industrial non–electrical equipment waste (INEW) [30], which helps to define the copper content in each strea

m. The industrial sector accounts for nearly 9% of total copper used in Asia [3]. Copper is employed in IEW in underground and undersea cables, surface cables and transformers, while in INEW it is used in ships, rail and aircraft, plants and machinery, among others [30]. Copper alloy tubes are also used in industrial applications, as these carry fluids in oil, chemical, process and marine industries. Other uses include water distribution, drainage, vents, irrigation and agricultural sprinklers, heating including solar, oxygen and non–flammable medical–gas systems. Copper alloys are also used in heat–exchange equipment, pressure vessels and vats; these can be used in highly demanding environments as well [2]. The amount of copper in industrial wastes can account up to 200 mg/kg [1]. The approaches used for recycling copper and copper alloys from industrial wastes are quite similar to that reported in construction and demolition section, being similar in relative composition and contamination with coatings and fluids, as well as the tubes and pipes scraps recovered from the C&D area. 

### **Municipal Solid Waste** 

Municipal solid waste by definition includes all refuse items from households, non–hazardous solid wastes, commercial and institutional establishments, such as hospitals, market and yard wastes and street sweepings [31]. Household waste approximately accounts for nearly 55% to 65% of the total MSW, while the contribution from commercial and institutional establishments can amount up to 35 to 45% [32]. Several materials contribute to the copper content in the MSW, such as daily household and commercial waste, large household appliances, motorcycles, printed circuit boards, automobile parts and furniture [33]. Other sources are copper arsenate used as a fungicide in wood preservation, copper phthalocyanine, employed as a blue pigment [33], cookware, brassware, locks, keys as well as coins [27]. Copper content in MSW can range from 360 to 700 mg/kg [1]. 

Incineration is one of the main processes used to treat and manage MSW. The main objective is to sterilise wastes as well as decrease the volume of material for disposal by up to 90%. Incinerators can also recover energy from wastes, which can be used for producing electricity or for heating [34]. In 1994, approximately 22% of MSW was incinerated in Europe [1]. Residual product streams after incineration include bottom ash and fly ash. The fly ash is collected from the air pollution system [34], with a copper content in the particulate matter between 1000 and 5000 mg/kg [1]. There are five ways to manage the fly ash, i.e., disposal as a hazardous material, solidification, chemical stabilisation, ash melting or vitrification and extraction/recovery processes [34]. The use of a particular technology depends on the associated costs and the nature of the product to be recovered.

### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

A heat treatment investigation was c

arried out in a high temperature horizontal tube furnace with an aim to recover copper from waste PCBs, provided by Steinert (Melbourne, Australia). The samples were heated at 1150°C for periods of 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8 and 10 minutes under high purity argon atmosphere at a rate of 1 L/min. The process consisted of preheating the sample in the cold zone for 5 minutes in the temperature range of 250°C – 350°C, followed by the heating at the temperature and times mentioned above. After the heat treatment, the sample was placed again into the cold zone of the furnace to avoid re–oxidation of the residue and thermal cracking. The residues recovered after heat treatment were analysed through Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) – Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS), Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICP) and LECO C and N analyser. 

### **RESULTS** 

Two types of residues were obtained after the heat treatment at all times: a gas fraction and a solid material. A detailed analysis of the solid residue is presented here. The solid residue had two well–defined components: a metallic phase and a carbonaceous residue. The total metallic phase consisted of a 54.36 wt. % copper, a 29.29 wt. % tin and a 8.85 wt. % lead. The remaining 7.5% were traces of other metals, such as Al, Au, Fe, Mg, Ni, Pd, Pt and Zn. The metallic phase was formed by silver and red coloured droplets; these were analysed with ICP technique; the silver droplets corresponded to tin/lead alloys and the red ones to copper–based alloys. SEM–EDS analyses were also carried out to obtain qualitative information about the residue. Results obtained showed that within the first two minutes of heat treatment, no metallic phase was formed, and copper could not be recovered. The recovery of copper took place with heat treatment times of 3 minutes and longer. Figure 1A shows an SEM analysis of a copper layer being part of the residue before phase separation and Figure 1B, the analysis of a copper droplet after the metallic phase.  Silver droplets were also analysed through SEM–EDS; the main components of these were tin and lead, with small quantities of copper, carbon and oxygen had separated from the waste (Figure 2).

### **DISCUSSION** 

Two types of metals were recovered from the high temperature heat treatment of waste PCBs: a copper–based alloy and a tin–lead alloy. SEM and ICP analyses of the copper droplets showed that the recovery of Cu as part of the metallic phase increased with the heat treatment time; longer the time of heat treatment, the higher the recovery, reaching > 90% after 5 minutes. Small quantities of other elements were found inside the copper droplets, such as lead, tin, oxygen and carbon. Cu–Sn [35] and Cu–Pb [36] phase diagrams show that the composition of the alloy formed is liquid and homogeneous at 1150°C, as it is above melting point of copper (1084.87°C) [37]. Traces of these elements were found inside the copper droplets as their melting points were lower than Cu melting point and they tend to form alloys with copper. 

Tin–lead alloys were also recovered after the heat treatment. These two metals have low melting points – 232°C and 327°C, respectively [38] – so this alloy can be formed at any composition and temperature above the lead melting point. Some copper was also found within the Sn–Pb droplets. 

Not all of copper was present in the metallic phase; a small fraction remained within the slag. This quantity of copper was oxidised according to equations 1 and 2 [39], which shows that the oxidation reaction is likely to occur, as it is exergonic. However, oxygen has a higher affinity with carbon and other slag–formative elements, making the reduction of copper easier at these temperatures. 



The generation of a slag phase is another important finding of this investigation. Several elements, including metals, remain in this oxides phase, as their reactions are likely to proceed at these temperatures. This issue can enhance the purity of the metallic phase, as no slag phase elements were found in the copper rich metallic phase. Some of the elements found in the slag residue were silicon, magnesium, aluminium and carbon.

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Copper is an essential commodity because of its extensive utilisation in different areas such as electrical and electronic products, building construction, costumer and general products, among others. As this metal is extracted from the earth’s crust, it is important to conserve this finite resource and seek alternative resources. A wide variety of copper waste re

sources are currently available for recycling and urban mining. With the concentration of metal in many cases being much higher than the corresponding ores, recovery of metal through recycling is becoming economically and environmentally feasible. Some of the advantages of recycling include the reduction in energy consumption as compared to the copper extraction from the ore, as well as a reduction in the amount of solid residues left in the extraction, a minimisation in the end–of–life wastes being landfilled, a decrease in the contamination of soil, water as well as air, and increased availability. 

A number of key results were obtained during experimental investigations on recycling of waste PCBs. The recovery of copper started from 3 minutes of heat treatment onwards, more than 90% recovery was achieved. Tin and lead were also distributed within the metallic phase, these were formed separately from copper–based alloy droplets. A second solid residue was generated, which was found to be predominantly a slag/carbonaceous phase, along with trace metals such as aluminium, silicon and magnesium, and up to ~30 wt. % carbon. 

A number of challenges facing the recovery of copper have been reported in this study. The importance of developing environmentally friendly processes that are technically as well as economically feasible has been discussed. Also, studies on mixtures of different types of wastes and their interaction will lead to important know– how to improve current processes and develop new ones. Another important issue that needs to be addressed is the impurities present in the metal phase from various waste streams, which could be present in a significant proportion and in the most of the cases these may be quite different from those present in copper ores. Their behaviour and influence on copper recovery needs to be understood. 

Not only the research community, but governments, legislation as well as the entire society needs to be a part of the recycling awareness towards managing resources. There is an urgent need for developing new technologies to meet the requirements of wastes treatment/management, which nowadays are becoming increasingly complex. This route of processing residues will lead to the reduction of wastes going to landfill, as well as develop new material resources.

### **CHEMISTRY** 

Oxygen added to molten copper will react with impurities, which will increase electrical conductivity.  This, however, happens only to a certain oxygen level; above that level, the conductivity will decrease.  Oxygen will also react with dissolved hydrogen and form steam, some of which can be entrapped in the solidifying bar as gas bubble and form porosity. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

366 

A study carried out by Southwire and described at a Wire Association meeting suggested the following for the wheel caster.  If Sb+Pb+S+Bi+Se+Te = 18 ppm or more and the oxygen level is 400 ppm or less, copper will be prone to hot cracking.  Pb and S in that equation can reach 12 ppm and 10 ppm, respectively, as shown by Chia, Seminar Notes [2]. 

Hitachi Cable used a variety of chemistries and carried-out a complete study which evaluated a wide range of impurity levels.  Hitachi also carried out a design experiment with varying impurity levels.  The addition of elements varied from 1 ppm to about 100 ppm.  The Hitachi experiments were carried out on a small

scale and were followed by a large, commercial-scale operation, as described in [3]. 

The oxygen level, based on the experiments, was set at maximum of 450 ppm, which is the welding requirement of 8-mm diameter rod.  Due to the high oxide concentration, wire breaks occurred when the oxygen exceeded 500 ppm. 

Several elements were selected as impurities:  lead, sulfur, bismuth, selenium, tellurium, tin, iron, silver, nickel, silicon, and antimony.  The experiments showed that this group could be divided into two separate categories: 

- Elements that caused rolling cracks after reaching certain level:  antimony, lead, sulfur, bismuth, selenium and tellurium. 

- Elements that did not cause rolling cracks regardless of their content:  tin, iron, silver, nickel, and silicon. 

The sensitivity of the bar to rolling fractures was a function of not only the amount of impurities but also to the structure of the cast bar.  The response of the bar with a columnar structure was very different from that of bar with an equiaxed grain structure. 

Small-scale experiments as well as large-scale commercial studies suggested that there was a much higher tolerance for impurities if the wires were drawn from the rod produced from fine, equiaxed bar rather than from large, columnar grain bar.  In fact, that tolerance was over three times as high.  The number of defects in the drawn wires was quantified by the use of the cold eddy current method. 

For example, if a columnar grain bar was cast with over 8 ppm of lead, there was a significant increase of defects.  However, if the same wire was drawn from rod produced from equiaxed grain bar, the tolerance limit was 25 ppm.  The same was true for all other impurities; much higher limits were possible when fine, equiaxed cast structure was obtained. 

This improved performance was most likely due to two major factors:  1) elements with low solid solubility in copper will precipitate at grain boundaries and cause cracking during rolling and 2) the redistribution of the harmful elements within the

cast structure will help prevent cracking at elevated impurity levels.  The length of the grain boundaries increased per unit of surface area.  As shown above, a fine structure can be obtained under controlled casting conditions. 

Adams and Chia, of Southwire, postulated somewhat similar approach in their 1982 invention, Patent No. 4,352,697:  "Method of Hot-Forming Metals Prone to Crack during Rolling" [4] where they suggested "forming a shell of finely distributed recrystallized grains in the surface layers of the cast bar by a selected small amount of deformation of the cast bar."  That first stage of bar preparation apparently allowed a second reduction to be taken without any bar cracking, even with a high impurity content. 

The La Farga Lacambra invention of 2000, Patent No. 6,797,082 [5], suggested the use of a "copper microalloy" with at least 200 ppm by weight

of lead and other impurities with content of tens ppm of weight.  They suggested that this alloy should be heated to 550°C – 650°C for 5 to 600 seconds. This would allow for the production of copper with a conductivity of 101.5% IACS.  This invention also claimed that the recrystallization temperature is lower than 200°C.  Therefore, the mechanical thermal and electrical properties of the rod were similar to that of ETP copper. 

The two inventions pertained to the wheel casting process.  It is more difficult to cast impure copper with a wheel caster due to severe bending of the bar.  The straightthrough mold of the Hazelett® twin-belt system with its 15-degree descending mold makes it easier for the bar to stay intact during solidification and its post-solidification condition. 

The lab model experiment performed by Hitachi was carried out with 11 impurities.  It was determined that lead, sulfur, bismuth, cerium, and tellurium incurred rolling cracks when the concentration of these elements exceeded a certain level. However, tin, silver and silicon, for example, did not cause rolling cracks with concentrations up to 300 ppm. 

The model experiments revealed rolling cracks when the concentration of lead was higher than 6 ppm, but the number of cracks rose abruptly when the concentration of lead increased to over 8 ppm.  Yet, another finding of these experiments showed that the number of cracks remained steady with a higher concentration of elements, such as tin and iron, for example. 

The model experiments were in very good agreement with the commercial production results. 

Further analysis of the model experiments found a correlation between the solid solubility of impurities and the rolling cracks.  That correlation was defined by solid solubility limits.  If the solid solubility of a certain element in the copper was less than 0.05%, it generated rolling cracks.  If the solid solubility of an element was higher than 5%, it did not generate any rolling cracks.

An obvious conclusion of these experiments was to lower the concentration of the impurities to less than the established tolerance limit and to reduce the volume of intermetallics at the grain boundaries. 

The fine, equiaxed copper bar structure is very helpful in distributing the impurities more evenly throughout the structure.  Since fine grains generate longer total grain boundary length when compared with the columnar grain boundary length, the concentration of the impurities per grain boundary unit length is lower.  As a result, the cracking tendency during rolling subsides. 

Quantitative experiments showed rather large differences between small grain structure, and large grain structure, in terms of the tendency to crack. 

Five types of impurities were used in the rolling experiments.  The original bar structure had 0.3-mm average grain diameter and was compared to a larger grain structure of 2.8 mm. 

In the case of lead

, for example, it was determined that the tolerance limit for cracking rose from 6 ppm to 22 ppm and, in the case of sulfur, from 8 ppm to 30 ppm. The tolerance limit of other impurities also increased. 

The number of defects in the rod was measured by an eddy current in-line detector.  The measurements during the actual production runs were in good agreement with the data obtained during lab experiments. 

In addition to casting experiments, Hitachi also performed another experiment which involved electromagnetic stirring of the holding furnace.  A stirrer was installed underneath the furnace to expose the impurities to the oxidizing atmosphere and to separate them at the surface of the melt. 

Three elements were traced:  lead, iron, and tin.  A very significant reduction in the amount of these impurities was noticed.  For example, the concentration of lead dropped from 60 ppm down to 10 ppm, when the stirring was used; similar results were obtained in the case of iron and tin. 

### **CONCLUSION** 

The Hitachi study was conducted to improve the understanding of the relationship between a scrap-based charge and the quality of rough-drawn wires. 

The study determined the concentration limits of various impurities at which the rough drawing could be performed without any detrimental effect on quality.  It was also concluded that a fine, as-cast structure tends to increase the range limits of impurities before they become harmful.

Rapid growth and technological advances in the use of electronic products have led to the generation of millions of tons of used electronics, commonly called “e-waste”. ### **INTRODUCTION** 

Consumer electronics have become an integral part of daily life and revolutionized the way we communicate, retrieve information, and entertain ourselves. Including cell phones, computers, televisions, iPads, and e-Readers, it has been estimated that the average person in North America uses 24 electronic products (CEA, 2008). Rapid technological advancements and growth in the electronics industry have led to a constant stream of new products and a resulting decrease in the life span of electronics. Globally, more than 50 million tons of e-waste was discarded in 2009 and 72 million tons are expected to be disposed in 2014 (Ping Jiang et al.). 

E-waste contains precious and special metals, including gold, silver, palladium and platinum, as well as potentially toxic substances such as lead, mercury, cadmium and beryllium. Therefore, responsible end-of-life management of e-waste is imperative in order to recover valuable components and properly manage hazardous and toxic components. End-of-life management of e-waste includes reuse of functional electronics, refurbishment and repair of electronics, recovery of electronic components, recycling e- waste, and disposal. Recycling of electronics allows for precious and special metals to be recovered, reduces the environmental impact associated with electronic manufacturing from raw materials, and ensures that hazardous and toxic substances are handled properly. Although there are clear benefits to recycling e-waste, the recycling rate is relatively low, due to inadequate recycling infrastructure. The global rate of e-waste recycling has been estimated at only 13% of the total e-waste stream in 2009 (Jiang et al.), while the estimates of recycling in the U.S. range from 14%<sup>1</sup> to 27%<sup>2</sup> . Based on the estimated U.S. generation of e-waste in 2010 of 2.2 million metr

It is estimated that 50 to 80 percent of the e-waste collected in the U.S. is exported to developing countries such as China, India and Pakistan, due to low-cost labor and less stringent environmental regulations (StEP), 2009) _._ The remaining e-waste is processed in copper smelters in Canada and Western Europe; the U.S. does not have integrated smelting capacity. These integrated smelters can process e-waste economically due to the advancement of the pyrometallurgical processes used and their ability to recover copper and precious metals from e-waste. Currently, the smelting and refining industry dominates e-waste recycling. Electronic devices contain up to 60 different elements, many of which are valuable, such as precious and special metals, and some of which are hazardous. Precious metals are rare, naturally occurring metallic elements, which traditionally have a higher melting point, and are more ductile than other metals. They have a high economic value, as demonstrated by the two most well known precious metals; gold and silver. ### **PYROMETALLURGICAL RECOVERY OF METALS** 

Copper is the most widely used metal in electronics due to its high electrical conductivity. Metals are often added to copper in order to change the strength, hardness, and/or resistance to corrosion. Copper alloys are metals that have copper as their main component (Copper Development Association (CDA)). The following is a list of the primary types of copper alloys: 

- (1) Bronze: Copper alloyed with tin, aluminum or silicon 

- (2) Brass: Copper alloyed with zinc 

- (3) Precious Metal Alloys: Copper alloyed with silver, gold, palladium, etc. 

Many metals dissolve in copper, including gold, silver, platinum, palladium, selenium and tellurium; therefore recovering metals from electronic waste focuses on smelting them to recover impure copper and then electrorefining the copper into pure copper and all other metals. Pyrometallurgical processing consists of melting electronic waste in a high temperature furnace, and is the most common process used for metal recovery from WEEE. This process is called “smelting” and is used to recover the copper content of electronic scrap plus any other “noble” metals that on melting dissolve in copper, such as silver, gold, platinum, and palladium. Iron and aluminum are not recovered in the copper smelting process, and instead are oxidized to slag. 

Electronic waste can be processed in small furnaces. However, the most common industrial process is to co-process them with copper sulphide concentrates in large copper smelting furnaces, such as copper converters, anode copper furnaces, and copper smelting and converting furnaces such as the Noranda Process. 

There are four global leaders in recovering metal values from e-waste by means of smelting and refining: Boliden, Xstrata Copper (formerly Noranda), Aurubis and Umicore. Global e-waste is primarily sent to four integrated smelters/refineries worldwide that process e-waste and recover precious metals ( _info_ Dev). Three of these are located in Europe – Belgium, Germany and Sweden – and one in Quebec in Canada. Moderately sized e-scrap smelters are also located in Japan and South Korea. The U.S does not have any treatment capacity despite being the largest producer of e-waste in the world. 

The need for e-waste recycling and processing capacity is widely recognized by the global leaders in smelting. In January 2008, Xstrata Copper announced plans to double electronic scrap recycling capacity at its Horne smelter, providing the smelter with the capacity to receive and process 100,000 metric per year. In April of 2010, Boliden announced that it would be investing SEK 1.3 billion ($202 million U.S. dollars) in order to triple its electronic scrap recycling capacity its Ronnskar smelter from 45,000 to 120,000 metric tons per year. expansion will allow for 2.7 million metric tons of e- waste to be recycled, and increase e-scrap’s share of Ronnskar’s raw material feeds from _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 376 6% to 14% (Boliden, 2010). At Xstrata’s Horne smelter, cathode ray tubes are completely recycled; the plastic tube is sent to a smelter, the glass is re-used at the facility as a fluxing agent, and the lead is recovered. 2. _Particle Size Reduction._ Once the electronics have been removed of their hazardous components, they are shredded into scrap metals and fines. The shredded material is then further separated using vibratory conveyors, shaker tables, cross-belt magnets, eddy current and sand flow units, among other density and/or magnetic separation methods. Dusts are generated during pre-treatment processes and are collected in filter and

bag-house systems. These dusts can have high precious metals content but also contain significant amounts of pollutants and high burn-loss components like plastics, paper and wood. The dusts can be sent to the smelting process for recovery of precious metals. 

It is common for high-grade e-waste not to go through mechanical shredding processes. At Umicore, shredding of mobile phones and computer circuit boards is not performed and devices are instead sent directly to integrated smelters. Shredding of high grade e-waste is not performed due to: 

   - The creation of precious metal containing dust. 

   - Significant losses of metals and components in side steams that cannot be recovered (such as plastic, aluminum, and iron). 

   - The economic value of precious metals far exceeds the value of base metals, such as iron and aluminum. It is not worth losing precious metals to recover base metals. 

   - Savings in time and money spent on pre-treatment. 

3. _Sample Assay._ E-scrap is sampled in order to assess copper and precious metals content. Separated materials are then sent to the smelter. 

### <u>End-Processing:</u> 

1. _Smelting Stage._ Shredded e-scrap is sent to an integrated smelter. A solution of copper and iron sulfide is produced (“matte”) while iron and other oxides form a silicate solution called “slag”. The precious metals are contained within the matte, which goes to the converting stage. The slag is treated separately through the use of a lead blast furnace, lead refinery and special metals plant. 

> 3 This general process was devised by comparing processing methods at Xstrata Copper, Boliden, and Umicore Precious Metals Refining. Please refer to Appendix A for a detailed explanation of processes at Xstrata Copper’s Horne Smelter, Boliden’s Ronnskar Smelter, and Umicore’s Hoboken Smelter. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

379 

It is important to note that high grade e-waste can be sent directly to the convertor and does not need to go through the smelting process. 

2. _Converting Stage._ The smelting stage is followed by a “converting” stage where matte is converted to impure copper, called “blister” copper. 

3. _Anode Furnace._ Liquid blister copper is then refined in the anode furnaces. The blister copper is cast into anodes that are then electrorefined to pure copper. 

4. _Electrorefining._ During this process, copper anodes are refined to produce pure copper cathodes and precious metals such as silver, gold, selenium and tellurium settle as precipitates at the bottom of the electrorefining cell. 

5. _Precious Metals Refinery._ The precious metal residue is then melted, casted and refined to produce precious metal bullion. 

Plastic components of e-waste cannot easily be recycled due to the mix of flame retardants, pigments and mixed types of plastics. However, smelting processes are able to use the energy content of the plastics. Energy usage is reduced due to the combustion of plastics and other flamm

able materials in the e-waste feed, which partially substitute the coke needed as a reducing agent and energy source. 

Although pyrometallurgical treatment is the most common method for recovering valuable metals from e-waste, there are some disadvantages: 

- Smelting cannot recover certain product components, such as chips or bare fiberglass boards. 

- Smelting cannot recover aluminum and iron since they are oxidized and transferred in the slag. 

- Smelting flame retardants and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) present in e-waste leads to the formation of dioxins, requiring special emission controls. 

- Pyrometallurgical processing cannot fully separate all metals, and therefore hydrometallurgical processing methods must be used subsequently. 

### **Pyrometallurgical Processing at Major Global Smelters** 

<u>The Horne Smelter of Xstrata Copper (Noranda, Quebec, Canada)</u> 

Xstrata Copper’s Horne Smelter has a capacity of approximately 714,000 metric tons of copper concentrates and other copper bearing materials per year. The facility accepts the following electronics: computers, peripherals, network hardware, tape drives, disk drives, modems, compact disks (CD), digital video disks (DVD), CD writers, circuit boards, copiers, cellular phones, telephones, typewriters, fax machines, printers, plotters, calculators, etc. 

Electronics to be sent to the Horne smelter from the U.S. are sampled at U.S. locations prior to being sent, in order to assess copper and precious metal content. Electronics are brought to the plant from across Canada and the U.S., where they are weighed and a bar code is assigned. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

380 

Hazardous electronic components, such as batteries, cathode ray tubes and mercury bulbs, are removed at designated sorting stations. Cathode ray tubes are separated into the plastic tube, the glass component, and lead. The plastic tube is sent to a smelter, the glass is re-used at the facility as a fluxing agent, and the lead is recovered. Batteries and ink cartridges are recycled, and plastics from these hazardous components are used as fuel for the facility. 

Once the electronics have been removed of their hazardous components, they are shredded into scrap metals and fines. The shredded material is then further separated using a vibrator conveyor and shaker table. Cross-belt magnets are used to separate fines and steel, and then an eddy current and sand flow unit is employed to separate aluminum from copper and plastics based on density differences. Materials such as scrap and residues are sampled based on the characteristics of each stream. 

Separated material is then sent to Xstrata’s Horne smelter in Quebec for further processing and metal recovery. The Horne smelter is a continuous primary smelting operation with a daily capacity of approximately 700 short tons of scrap per day. There are three major stages of smelting which occur in the Noranda Process reactor, converters and the anode fur

naces. The smelting process oxidizes iron, lead and zinc into a silicabased slag, which is cooled and milled to recover precious metals. The precious metals, which are contained in the copper matte, are transferred from the furnace to the converters. Liquid blister copper is then refined in the anode furnaces, producing A-grade copper anodes of 99.1% copper. The remaining 0.9% contains precious metals such as gold, silver and palladium, along with selenium, tellurium and nickel. These metals are recovered in the subsequent electro-refining process where the impure anode copper is dissolved and deposited on cathode sheets while the impurities contained in the anode are recovered as “copper slimes”. The electrolytic refining produces 99.99% pure copper cathodes. Precious metals are separated from the copper slimes collected in the bottom of the electrorefining tank. The residue is melted, casted and refined to produce silver and gold bullion on site. Additional byproducts recovered include platinum, palladium, tellurium, and selenium. 

Energy usage in the Noranda reactor is reduced due to the combustion of plastics in the e-waste feedstock. 

### <u>Boliden’s Ronnskar Smelter (Skelleftehamn, Sweden)</u> 

Boliden’s Ronnskar Smelter is Boliden’s largest unit and the world’s largest recycler of copper and precious metals from e-scrap. Boliden’s expansion of Ronnskar’s scrap handling capacity from 45,000 to 120,000 metric tons per year has increased the e- scrap share of Ronnskar’s raw material feeds from 6% to 14%.  Recycling of e-waste will produce approximately 22,000 metric tons of copper, 80,000 kilograms of silver and 7,500 kilograms of gold (Boliden, 2010). The majority of the e-scrap sent to Ronnskar comes from Europe and North America.

In addition to refining metals from e-waste, the Ronnskar Smelter refines metals from copper scrap, copper/zinc residues, electric arc furnace dust, and lead scrap. The total capacity of the Ronnskar smelter is approximately 857,000 metric tons per year, and Ronnskar has an annual production of more than 200,000 metric tons of copper, 13,000 kg of gold and 400,000 kg of silver. 

Low grade e-waste is first fed into the Kaldo Furnace, which produces a mixed copper alloy and dusts. The mixed copper alloy is sent to the convertor for recovery of copper, gold, silver, palladium, nickel, selenium and zinc, while the dusts (Pb, Sb, In and Cd) are sent for further metals recovery. High grade e-waste is sent directly to the convertor and does not need to go through the Kaldo Furnace.

- Very low grade: gold content of lower than 50 ppm 

- • Components ranging from ICs to small entire devices (i.e. mobile phones): 

Umicore’s process is to remove batteries and then treat material directly in their integrated smelter/refinery without shredding or sorting into fractions before treatment. This direct form of treatment reduced the losses of valuable metals into side streams (Fe-, Al-, plastics, etc.), and saves money that would have been spent on pre-treatment costs. 

In small devices such as mobile phones, the value of the precious metals generally far exceeds the value of the iron and aluminum they contain. In addition, their plastic components cannot be feasibly recycled due to the mix of flame retardants, pigments and mixed types of plastics. Umicore’s integrated smelting/refining process recovers Sn, Pb, In, etc. from mobile phones and uses the energy content of the plastics. 

Computers require manual dismantling and mechanical pre-processing in order to separate and sort the various fractions. During mechanical pre-processing stages, large volumes of mixed plastic fractions are generated. It is not economically feasible to separate and recover these types of plastics. However, Umicore can process mixed plastic fraction in order to recover copper, precious metals, etc. while at the same time using the organic content of the plastics to replace the fuel used in this process. 

Du

sts are generated during pre-treatment processes and are collected in filter and bag-house systems. These dusts can have high precious metals content but also contain significant amounts of pollutants and high burn-loss components like plastics, paper and wood. Umicore is able to process these dusts depending on the quality and quantity of precious metals. 

### **CONCLUSION** 

The amount of e-waste generated globally contains both precious and potentially hazardous  metals and, therefore, there are both resource conservation and environmental reasons to collect it and process it properly. Collection depends on citizens separating e- waste and bringing it to designated centers. At this time, collection is hampered by lack of adequate information and infrastructure. With regard to processing, the most economic route is pyrometallurgical treatment in either copper concentrate smelters, such as the Noranda process at Noranda Quebec, or secondary copper smelters, followed by electrorefining recovery of the metals contained in the anode copper. Most of the U.S. e- waste goes to landfills so there I a dire need to provide a sorting infrastructure and e- waste smelting capacity.

### **COPPER EXTRACTION FROM WASTE PRINTED CIRCUIT BOARDS** 

D. E. Chaverra and O. J. Restrepo _National University of Colombia Calle 59 No 63 – 20 Medellнn, Colombia dechaverraa@unal.edu.co, ojrestre@unal.edu.co_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

The waste stream of Electrical and Electronic Equipment (EEE) is growing, because the market is far from saturated and the time of use of EEEs is decreasing as a result of technological innovation. The printed circuit boards (PCB) are the basis for the electronics industry, being an essential part of almost all EEE. They are a material of growing interest, not only for its metal content, about 20 % of copper, but also by the complications during recovery of metals due to its complex composition and lack of established methods. 

A method for the recovery of copper from waste PCBs of computers, as a first contribution to a process of complete recycling of electronic is proposed. The process consists on a size reduction and classification, magnetic and electrostatic separation, sulfuric acid leaching and final obtaining process. The methodology is developed at laboratory level achieving a concentrate containing about 60 % of copper and an extraction of 88 % after leaching.

### **INT

RODUCTION** 

Electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) have presented a rapid development in recent decades, proportionally, has increased the number of these that are discarded as a result the flow of waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) are every day increasing. About 20 and 50 million tons of WEEEs are produced worldwide each year, with an of 3-5 % [1]. This presents an emerging environmental problem and a challenge for the development of sustainable processing technologies that are able to cope with the volume and complexity of the WEEEs, with low-cost and environmentally sensitive methods [2-3]. 

In recent years recycling has become an alternative, even regarded as the best option [4]. It consists of the dismantling, removal of hazardous elements, size reduction by knife mills and pulverizes, and concentration by gravimetric processes, magnetic and electrostatic separation processes, and others [5–9]. All these processes are done in order to release the metal bound or encapsulated with resin and ceramic, and improve the speed of the following processes. They are suitable from the standpoint of environmental [10]. 

Metals have been recycled from electronic waste by high-temperature processes such as melting and pyrolysis, which presented pollutant emissions and slag formation with multiple metal content where recovery becomes complicated [11]. In the last decade, attention has focused on aqueous processes, which represent a promising option because of the relatively low capital costs, reduced environmental impacts, potential for high metal recoveries, and are suitable methods for application on a small scale [1]. The main proposals consist on leaching using aqua regia, cyanide, thiosulfate, thiourea or halides [4], [12-13]. For the extraction of copper have been studied various processes in aqueous solution using sulfuric acid [14], chlorine [13], [15-16], nitric acid and solvent extraction [11], [17], ammonia-ammonium sulfate and chloride systems [18–20], reaching copper recoveries above of 71 %. 

In this paper we developed and implemented a process for the recovery of copper from printed circuit boards (PCB) of electronic wastes. The method was performed using physical and mechanical processes, along with chemical techniques of extractive metallurgy. The process is proposed as a viable alternative to copper recovery from WEEEs, thus contributing to the solving the problem of end disposal of electronic wastes. 

### **MATERIAL AND METHODS** 

For experimental development were processed 4300 g of material consisting on video cards, motherboards, modems, RAM modules, and hard disk controller boards. Parts of different trademarks as a representative sample were taken. Three samples were taken from each resulting stream throughout the process, dissolved in aqua regia and copper analysis was done by atomic absorption spectroscopy with an AA Spectrometer iCE 300 SERIES Thermo SCIENTIFIC equipment. ### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The physical processes of magnetic and electrostatic concentration are a good alternative for the extraction of copper from the PCB wastes, achieving an average recovery of 73 %. On the other hand, are suitable because they do not generate pollution, because there are no particle emissions and effluents with hazardous substances. 

A copper recovery of 88 % is obtained, operating at a sulfuric acid concentration of 2M, hydrogen peroxide volume 20 mL/100 mL, solid amount of 50 g/L at room temperature. 

After a filtering process the copper is obtained by electrowinning and the solutions can be sent to the leaching processes. The solid residue can be processed to recover other metals like gold and silver. Unrefined copper is obtained with a purity exceeding 99 %. 

The total process recovery was 68 %, indicating that this process, which use physical and chemical operations typical of mineral processing, is a viable alternative for copper recovery from PCB wastes, reducing the end disposal problems of electronic wastes.

P. Rodenas Motos, R.J.W. Meulepas, T.H.J.A. Sleutels, M. Saakes and A. ter Heijne _Wetsus, centre of excellence for sustainable water technology Agora 1_ **_,_** _8934 CJ Leeuwarden, the Netherlands roel.meulepas@wetsus.nl_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Metals are commonly removed from wastewater by precipitation, e.g. with slaked lime, resulting in the production of large amounts of with metal contaminated waste. The annual global production of mine wastes has been estimated at approximately 15,00020,000 million tons. 

This paper presents a novel process to recover metals from metallurgical wastewaters or mine drainage. The process is driven by the chemical energy present in waste streams that contain reduced compounds, like organics or sulphide. The process comprises an electrochemical cell in which the anode and cathode are separated by a membrane. At the anode, electrochemically-active microorganisms oxidise the organic matter or reduced sulphur compounds. At the cathode, dissolved metals are reduced to their elemental form, similar to electrowinning. Because the potential for organic matter or sulphide oxidation is lower than the potential for copper reduction the reaction is spontaneous.
